Each appendix is self-contained and can be referenced independently. Use the sidebar to jump directly to the resource you need.

Beyond the specific appendices provided, we recommend: Joining the Physical AI community forums Exploring the official ROS 2 and Isaac platform documentation Participating in open-source robotics projects Let's ensure you have all the tools and knowledge needed to succeed!
Estimated Reading Time: 12 minutes Prerequisites: Basic Linux knowledge Difficulty: Beginner

You don't need expensive hardware to learn robotics. Cloud providers offer powerful GPUs by the hour. You pay only for what you use. This guide shows you how to set up AWS for robotics development. You'll learn to run ROS 2, train models, and test in simulation. All without buying hardware. By the end, you'll have a complete cloud development environment.

No Upfront Cost: Don't spend $2,000+ on a workstation. Start for $1/hour. Latest Hardware: Access newest GPUs immediately. No waiting for hardware delivery. Scalability: Need more power? Scale up instantly. Done training? Scale down. Collaboration: Share environments easily. Multiple people can access the same setup.

Ongoing Costs: $50-200/month adds up over time. Network Latency: Remote desktop has slight lag. No Offline Work: Need internet connection. Cannot Deploy to Physical Robots: Cloud can't directly control local hardware.

Type: Comparison Context: You're deciding between buying a $2,000 workstation or using cloud. Explanation: Workstation: $2,000 upfront. Use it 2 years. Cost: $83/month equivalent. Cloud: $100/month. Use it 6 months while learning. Then buy hardware. Total: $600. Cloud is cheaper for learning. Buy hardware later when you know what you need. Takeaway: Cloud is cost-effective for learning and experimentation.
Go to aws.amazon.com Click "Create an AWS Account" Provide email and payment info Important: Set up billing alerts immediately!

Don't skip this! Prevent surprise bills. Go to AWS Billing Dashboard Click "Billing preferences" Enable "Receive Billing Alerts" Set alerts for: $50 (warning) $100 (serious warning) $200 (stop everything!)

AWS offers many GPU instances. Here's what matters for robotics: g5.xlarge ($1.01/hour)​ GPU: NVIDIA A10G (24GB VRAM) CPU: 4 vCPUs RAM: 16GB Best for: Light development, testing g5.2xlarge ($1.21/hour) - Recommended​ GPU: NVIDIA A10G (24GB VRAM) CPU: 8 vCPUs RAM: 32GB Best for: Development, model training g6.xlarge ($0.94/hour)​ GPU: NVIDIA L4 (24GB VRAM) CPU: 4 vCPUs RAM: 16GB Best for: Budget-conscious development Monthly cost estimate (4 hours/day, 5 days/week): ~$100

Go to EC2 Dashboard Click "Launch Instance" Choose "Deep Learning AMI (Ubuntu 22.04)" Select instance type (g5.2xlarge recommended) Configure storage: 100GB minimum Configure security group: Allow SSH (port 22) from your IP Allow Custom TCP (port 5901) for VNC Create/select key pair Click "Launch" Wait 2-3 minutes for instance to start.

# Download your key pair (yourkey.pem) chmod 400 yourkey.pem # Connect to instance ssh -i yourkey.pem ubuntu@<your-instance-ip> Replace <your-instance-ip> with your actual instance IP from AWS console.

# Update system sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y # Add ROS 2 repository sudo curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ros/rosdistro/master/ros.key -o /usr/share/keyrings/ros-archive-keyring.gpg echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/ros-archive-keyring.gpg] http://packages.ros.org/ros2/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo $UBUNTU_CODENAME) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ros2.list > /dev/null # Install ROS 2 sudo apt update sudo apt install ros-humble-desktop -y # Source ROS 2 echo "source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash" >> ~/.bashrc source ~/.bashrc
# Install Gazebo Harmonic sudo apt install ros-humble-ros-gz -y
# Install Python tools pip install numpy scipy matplotlib # Install ROS 2 tools sudo apt install python3-colcon-common-extensions -y

VS Code makes cloud development feel local. On your local machine: Install VS Code Install "Remote - SSH" extension Press F1, type "Remote-SSH: Connect to Host" Enter: ubuntu@<your-instance-ip> Select your key file when prompted Now you can edit code as if it's local!

Some tools need GUI (like RViz). Use VNC: On cloud instance: # Install VNC server sudo apt install tigervnc-standalone-server tigervnc-common -y # Set VNC password vncpasswd # Start VNC server vncserver :1 -geometry 1920x1080 -depth 24 On your local machine: # Create SSH tunnel ssh -L 5901:localhost:5901 -i yourkey.pem ubuntu@<your-instance-ip> # Connect with VNC viewer to localhost:5901 Use any VNC client (RealVNC, TigerVNC Viewer, etc.).

Type: Decision Guide Context: You're not sure whether to use VS Code Remote or VNC. Explanation: For code editing and terminal work: Use VS Code Remote. It's faster and feels native. For GUI tools (RViz, Gazebo GUI): Use VNC. GUI needs graphical display. Best approach: Use both! VS Code for code, VNC for visualization. Takeaway: Different tools for different needs. Use the right tool for each task.

Gazebo can run without GUI: # Set environment for software rendering export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 # Launch Gazebo headless gz sim --headless-rendering your_world.sdf This uses CPU rendering. Slower but works without display.
For better performance: # Use VNC session # Inside VNC, run: gz sim your_world.sdf GUI shows in VNC window. GPU accelerates rendering.
# In VNC session ros2 run rviz2 rviz2 RViz appears in your VNC window.

Cloud GPUs are powerful. Use them for training: # Example: Training a perception model python train_model.py --batch-size 32 --epochs 100 # GPU will be used automatically # Monitor with: nvidia-smi Check GPU usage: watch -n 1 nvidia-smi This shows GPU memory, utilization, and temperature.

Spot instances cost 70% less! But AWS can terminate them. When to use spots: Long training jobs (save checkpoints!) Experimentation Non-urgent work When NOT to use spots: Demos or presentations Critical deadlines

Critical: Stop instance after work! # Before logging off sudo poweroff Or use AWS console: Instance → Actions → Stop Cost comparison: Running 24/7: $730/month (g5.2xlarge) Running 4 hours/day: $97/month Savings: $633/month!
If you'll use cloud long-term: Commit to $X/month usage Get 20-40% discount Flexible across instance types
Delete: Old snapshots Unused volumes (storage) Stopped instances you don't need Check monthly: AWS → Cost Explorer
# From your local machine scp -i yourkey.pem your_data.tar.gz ubuntu@<instance-ip>:~/
# To your local machine scp -i yourkey.pem ubuntu@<instance-ip>:~/results.tar.gz ./

Use S3 for storage: # Install AWS CLI sudo apt install awscli -y # Upload to S3 aws s3 cp large_file.tar.gz s3://your-bucket/ # Download from S3 aws s3 cp s3://your-bucket/large_file.tar.gz ./ S3 costs ~$0.023/GB/month. Much cheaper than EBS volumes.
Problem: VNC feels laggy. Solution: Use VS Code Remote for code. Only use VNC when needed.
Problem: Cloud can't directly connect to your local robot. Solution: Develop in cloud. Deploy to local Jetson. Test on physical robot locally.
Problem: Large dataset transfers cost money. Solution: Keep datasets in S3. Don't download/upload repeatedly.

Problem: SSH disconnects when laptop sleeps. Solution: Use tmux or screen for persistent sessions: # Start tmux session tmux new -s mysession # Your work here... # Detach: Ctrl+B, then D # Reconnect: tmux attach -t mysession
Only allow SSH from your IP: In Security Group: Type: SSH Source: My IP (not 0.0.0.0/0!)
Never use password authentication. AWS uses keys by default. Keep it that way.
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y Do this weekly.
Check AWS Billing Dashboard daily. Catch problems early.
Price: $0.60-$1.10/hour Pros: Simpler than AWS, cheaper Cons: Limited availability
Price: Similar to AWS Pros: Good AI/ML tools Cons: More complex setup
Price: $0.51/hour+ Pros: Simpler interface Cons: Fewer GPU options
Problem: Ran out of disk space. Solution: Increase EBS volume size in AWS console.
Problem: VNC connection refused. Solution: Check security group allows port 5901. Check VNC server is running.
Problem: Forgot to stop instance! Solution: Set up billing alerts. Stop instances immediately. Request AWS billing support.

Cloud enables zero-hardware robotics development AWS g5 instances are perfect for ROS 2 and AI VS Code Remote for code, VNC for GU I Stop instances when not in use (critical!) Set billing alerts before starting Spot instances save 70% for training Cloud is ideal for learning, testing, and training

Development environments can be messy. You install packages. They conflict. A teammate can't run your code. Their system is different. Dev Containers solve this. They create identical environments for everyone. You define it once. Everyone uses it. No more "works on my machine." By the end, you'll have a working dev environment. You'll understand Docker. You'll understand Dev Containers. You'll use them for robotics.

A Dev Container is your development environment in a box. What it includes: Your code editor (VS Code) All required tools (ROS 2, Python, compilers) Libraries and dependencies Environment variables and settings Everything runs inside Docker. Docker is like a lightweight virtual machine. It isolates your environment. Your host system stays separate.

Type: Analogy Context: You want to bake a cake. Your friend wants the same cake. Explanation: Without a dev container, you give instructions. Get flour. Get eggs. Get sugar. Use an oven. But your friend might use different brands. Different oven temperature. The cake comes out wrong. With a dev container, you give a complete box. It has exact ingredients. It has the right oven. They open it. They bake. Perfect cake every time. Same result. Takeaway: Dev Containers package everything you need. They eliminate environment differences.
Everyone uses the same tools. Same ROS 2 version. Same Python version. Same libraries. No surprises.
New team member? They clone the repo. Open in VS Code. Click "Reopen in Container." Done. They're productive in minutes.
Your system stays clean. Don't pollute your host OS. Need different ROS versions? No problem. Each project has its own container.
Windows, Mac, Linux. Doesn't matter. Docker runs the same way. Your dev environment is portable.

Ubuntu/Linux: # Install Docker Engine curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh sudo sh get-docker.sh # Add your user to docker group (no sudo needed) sudo usermod -aG docker $USER # Log out and log back in for changes to take effect Windows/Mac: Download Docker Desktop from docker.com Install and run Docker Desktop Ensure it's running (check system tray)
In VS Code: Click Extensions (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + X) Search "Dev Containers" Install the extension by Microsoft

A typical setup looks like this: your_project/ ├── .devcontainer/ │ ├── devcontainer.json # Main config │ ├── Dockerfile # Container image │ └── post-create.sh # Setup script ├── src/ # Your code └── README.md The .devcontainer folder defines everything.
Here's a complete setup. This works for ROS 2 Humble development.

.devcontainer/devcontainer.json // Library: Dev Containers v0.362.0 // Last updated: 2025-12-05 // Tested on: VS Code 1.95, Docker 24.0 { "name": "ROS 2 Humble Development", "build": { "dockerfile": "Dockerfile", "args": { "ROS_DISTRO": "humble" } }, // VS Code settings "customizations": { "vscode": { "extensions": [ "ms-python.python", "ms-python.vscode-pylance", "ms-vscode.cpptools", "twxs.cmake", "ms-iot.vscode-ros" ], "settings": { "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "/usr/bin/python3", "python.linting.enabled": true, "python.linting.pylintEnabled": true } } }, // Forward ROS 2 and RViz ports "forwardPorts": [11311, 33691], // Run after container is created "postCreateCommand": "bash .devcontainer/post-create.sh", // Environment variables "containerEnv": { "ROS_DOMAIN_ID": "42" }, // Mount your workspace "workspaceFolder": "/workspace", "workspaceMount": "source=${localWorkspaceFolder},target=/workspace,type=bind", // Keep container running "overrideCommand": false, // GPU support (optional) "runArgs": ["--network=host"], // User settings "remoteUser": "ros" }

.devcontainer/Dockerfile # Library: Docker 24.0, ROS 2 Humble # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: Ubuntu 22.04 FROM osrf/ros:humble-desktop-full # Avoid prompts during package installation ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive # Install development tools RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \ python3-pip \ python3-colcon-common-extensions \ python3-rosdep \ git \ vim \ wget \ curl \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* # Install Python packages RUN pip3 install \ numpy \ scipy \ matplotlib \ transforms3d # Create a non-root user ARG USERNAME=ros ARG USER_UID=1000 ARG USER_GID=$USER_UID RUN groupadd --gid $USER_GID $USERNAME \ && useradd --uid $USER_UID --gid $USER_GID -m $USERNAME \ && apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y sudo \ && echo $USERNAME ALL=\(root\) NOPASSWD:ALL > /etc/sudoers.d/$USERNAME \ && chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/$USERNAME \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* # Set up ROS 2 workspace RUN mkdir -p /workspace/src WORKDIR /workspace # Source ROS 2 in bashrc RUN echo "source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash" >> /home/$USERNAME/.bashrc \ && echo "if [ -f /workspace/install/setup.bash ]; then source /workspace/install/setup.bash; fi" >> /home/$USERNAME/.bashrc # Switch to non-root user USER $USERNAME CMD ["/bin/bash"]

.devcontainer/post-create.sh #!/bin/bash # Library: bash 5.1 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: Ubuntu 22.04 source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash sudo rosdep init || true rosdep update if [ -d "/workspace/src" ] && [ "$(ls -A /workspace/src)" ]; then cd /workspace colcon build --symlink-install source install/setup.bash echo "Workspace built successfully!" else echo "No packages found in /workspace/src. Ready for development!" fi This script sets up ROS 2. It builds your workspace automatically. Make it executable: chmod +x .devcontainer/post-create.sh

Create the files: Copy the config files above. Open in VS Code: Open your project folder. Reopen in Container: Press F1 Type "Dev Containers: Reopen in Container" Press Enter Wait for build: First time takes 5-10 minutes. Docker downloads the image. Then it builds. Start coding: You're inside now. Everything is ready.

Start working: Open VS Code It remembers your container Click "Reopen in Container" if needed Build your code: cd /workspace colcon build source install/setup.bash Run ROS 2 nodes: ros2 run your_package your_node Stop working: Close VS Code Container stops automatically

Type: Scenario Context: You clone a robotics project. It has a .devcontainer folder. You never used this project. Explanation: You open the project in VS Code. VS Code detects the .devcontainer folder. It asks "Reopen in Container?" You click yes. VS Code builds the container. This takes a few minutes. Then you're inside. You run ros2 topic list. It works. You run colcon build. It builds successfully. No manual installation needed. No configuration required. The container has everything. Next week, a new teammate joins. They do the same thing. Same experience. Identical environment. Takeaway: Dev Containers eliminate setup time. They make onboarding instant.

documents.t: Gazebo and other simulators need GPU access. Enable it:

Install NVIDIA Container Toolkit: First, add the NVIDIA package repository: distribution=$(. /etc/os-release;echo $ID$VERSION_ID) curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/$distribution/libnvidia-container.list | \ sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | \ sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list Then install the toolkit: sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-container-toolkit Finally, restart Docker: sudo systemctl restart docker Update devcontainer.json: { "runArgs": [ "--gpus", "all", "--network=host" ], "containerEnv": { "NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES": "all", "NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES": "all" } } Test GPU: Inside the container, run: nvidia-smi You should see your GPU. It will show memory and usage.
GPU passthrough is limited on Windows and Mac. For serious simulation, you have two options. First, use a Linux host. Second, use cloud GPU instances. See Cloud Path for cloud setup.
You can add tools to your container. Edit the Dockerfile: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \ htop \ tmux \ tree \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
Add extensions to devcontainer.json: "extensions": [ "ms-python.python", "eamodio.gitlens", "donjayamanne.githistory" ] These load automatically when you open the container.
Install Python packages in the Dockerfile: RUN pip3 install \ opencv-python \ torch \ tensorboard
Set variables in devcontainer.json: "containerEnv": { "ROS_DOMAIN_ID": "42", "GAZEBO_MODEL_PATH": "/workspace/models" } These are available in all terminal sessions.

Need multiple ROS 2 versions? Create separate dev containers. Each project gets its own folder: your_projects/ ├── project_humble/ │ └── .devcontainer/ # ROS 2 Humble ├── project_iron/ │ └── .devcontainer/ # ROS 2 Iron └── project_jazzy/ └── .devcontainer/ # ROS 2 Jazzy Each project has its own environment. No conflicts happen.

For complex setups with multiple services: .devcontainer/docker-compose.yml # Library: Docker Compose v2.21 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: Docker 24.0 version: '3.8' services: robot: build: context: . dockerfile: Dockerfile volumes: - ..:/workspace:cached network_mode: host command: /bin/bash database: image: postgres:15 environment: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: robotics ports: - "5432:5432" Then update devcontainer.json. Reference the compose file: { "dockerComposeFile": "docker-compose.yml", "service": "robot", "workspaceFolder": "/workspace" } This connects multiple services together.
Problem: "Failed to start container" Solutions: First, check if Docker is running: docker ps Check disk space: docker system df Clean old containers: docker system prune

Problem: Building takes forever. Solutions: Docker caches layers. This speeds up builds. Don't change the Dockerfile often. Put frequently changing commands at the end. Use .dockerignore to exclude large files.

Problem: Robot USB devices not visible. Solution: Add device passthrough. Update your config: "runArgs": [ "--device=/dev/ttyUSB0:/dev/ttyUSB0", "--privileged" ] This allows container access to USB devices.
Problem: "Port 11311 already allocated" Solution: Stop the conflicting container. First, find running containers: docker ps Then stop the one using the port: docker stop <container_id>
Don't install everything. Only add what you need. Smaller containers are better. They build faster. They use less disk space.
Create a .dockerignore file. This excludes unnecessary files. Add these lines: .dockerignore .git .vscode build/ install/ log/ *.pyc __pycache__/ Docker will skip these files. Builds become faster.
Commit .devcontainer/ to git. This is important. Your whole team gets the same environment. No setup differences.
Add a README file. Explain these things: Required Docker version GPU requirements Special setup steps
Rebuild occasionally. This catches issues early. In VS Code, use this command: "Dev Containers: Rebuild Container" Do this monthly. Or after major changes.
To see container logs: docker logs <container_name> VS Code shows build logs. Check the Output panel.
First, find your container: docker ps Then access the shell: docker exec -it <container_name> /bin/bash
Remove all containers and images: docker system prune -a --volumes Then rebuild in VS Code. Use this command: "Dev Containers: Rebuild Container Without Cache" This gives you a fresh start.

Dev Containers solve environment problems. Everyone gets the same setup. No more "works on my machine" issues. Key benefits: VS Code integration makes it easy to use Isolation keeps your host system clean GPU support enables simulation and training Fully customizable to fit your needs Perfect for teams and complex projects

You now know how to set up dev containers. They give you consistent environments. They save time. They reduce errors. Next, learn how to troubleshoot common issues. Continue to: Troubleshooting FAQ Related topics: Cloud Path Hardware Guide Jetson BOM

Choosing hardware for robotics can be overwhelming. There are many options. Prices range from hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars. This guide helps you choose the right hardware. It covers three budget tiers. Each tier supports the projects in this book. By the end, you'll know exactly what to buy. You'll understand what each component does.
The short answer: Not immediately. This book focuses on simulation first. You can complete most projects without buying any hardware. Use your existing computer plus cloud resources.

Buy hardware when you: Want to deploy to real robots Need faster inference than cloud provides Want to test real-world sensor data Have completed simulation projects Start with simulation. Buy hardware later.

Type: Scenario Context: Maria starts learning robotics. She wonders if she should buy a $10,000 robot first. Explanation: Maria starts with simulation. She learns ROS 2. She builds projects. She tests algorithms. After 3 months, she knows exactly what hardware she needs. She buys a $1,500 Jetson kit. This is smarter than buying expensive hardware upfront. The hardware might not match her needs. Takeaway: Learn in simulation first. Buy hardware when you know what you need.
Choose a tier based on your budget and goals.

Best for: Students, hobbyists, beginners Core Components: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Dev Kit ($499) Intel RealSense D435 camera ($179) Basic accessories ($200-$300) Cloud GPU credits for training ($10-20/month) What you can do: Run perception models Test object detection Deploy VLA models Control simulated robots Limitations: Slower training times Limited to smaller models No physical robot Total: $700-$1,500 one-time + $10-20/month for cloud

Best for: Serious learners, researchers, small teams Core Components: NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin ($1,999) Intel RealSense D455 ($329) Desktop with RTX 4070 ($1,200-$1,800) Optional: Unitree Go2 quadruped ($2,700) What you can do: Train medium models locally Run multiple models simultaneously Test on real quadruped robot Faster inference Limitations: Still need cloud for heavy training Quadruped, not humanoid Total: $3,500-$5,000 (without robot) or $6,200-$7,700 (with robot)

Best for: Professional developers, companies, research labs Core Components: NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB ($2,999) Unitree G1 humanoid ($16,000) Workstation with RTX 4090 ($3,000-$4,000) High-end sensors ($1,000-$2,000) What you can do: Everything Train large models locally Deploy to humanoid robot Production-ready systems Total: $22,000-$28,000

Type: Decision Guide Context: You have $2,000 to spend. Should you buy the Economy or Mid-Range path? Explanation: If you're just learning: Buy Economy ($700). Save $1,300 for later upgrades. If you've completed simulation projects: Buy Mid-Range desktop ($1,800). This speeds up development significantly. If you want a real robot: Save more money first. Robots need infrastructure and maintenance. Takeaway: Match hardware to your current skill level, not your aspirations.

documents.t: Have you ever wondered how robots can walk, see, and interact with the physical world? Welcome to the exciting field of Physical AI – where artificial intelligence meets the real world through robotic bodies. This book will guide you from complete beginner to capable practitioner in Physical AI and Humanoid Robotics. You'll learn how modern robots perceive their environment, make decisions, and take action. By the end, you'll have hands-on experience building systems that control humanoid robots using cutting-edge AI models.
Before diving into the technical modules, let's establish what Physical AI really means and why it matters.

Physical AI is artificial intelligence that interacts with the physical world through robotic embodiment. Unlike traditional AI that operates purely in digital spaces, Physical AI must: Perceive the unpredictable real world through sensors Reason about physical constraints and dynamics Act through mechanical actuators with real-world consequences Adapt to changing environments in real-time

Every Physical AI system follows this fundamental cycle: Sense: Gather data from the environment (cameras, LIDAR, IMUs, touch sensors) Think: Process sensor data and make decisions (perception, planning, control) Act: Execute actions through motors and actuators (walking, grasping, speaking) This cycle repeats continuously, often 10-1000 times per second depending on the task.

Hardware: Sensors: Eyes and ears of the robot (cameras, LIDAR, microphones, IMUs) Actuators: Muscles of the robot (motors, servos, grippers) Compute: Brain of the robot (Jetson, laptops, cloud GPUs) Power: Battery systems and power management Software Stack: Operating System: Linux (typically Ubuntu) Middleware: ROS 2 for robot communication Simulation: Gazebo, Isaac Sim for virtual testing AI Models: Vision models, language models, control policies Applications: High-level task planning and execution

simple_robot_command.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import String class SimpleRobotController(Node): """A basic robot controller that publishes commands.""" def __init__(self): super().__init__('simple_robot_controller') # Create publisher for robot commands self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'robot_commands', 10) # Create timer that calls our callback every second self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.send_command) self.get_logger().info('Robot controller started!') def send_command(self): """Send a command to the robot.""" msg = String() msg.data = 'Walk forward' self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Sent command: {msg.data}') def main(): rclpy.init() controller = SimpleRobotController() rclpy.spin(controller) # Keep node running controller.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() Don't worry if this code looks unfamiliar! Welcome to Module 1! This is where you learn ROS 2. ROS 2 stands for Robot Operating System 2. It's the nervous system for modern robots. Think about your own nervous system. It sends messages between your brain and body. ROS 2 does the same thing for robots. It lets different robot parts talk to each other. By the end of this module, you'll understand how robots communicate. You'll also build your own robot programs.

ROS 2 is middleware for robots. Middleware is software that connects different programs. It helps them work together. ROS 2 provides three main things: Communication tools: Let robot parts send messages Libraries: Pre-built code for common robot tasks Tools: Programs to test and debug your robot

Type: Analogy Context: Imagine a humanoid robot trying to pick up a cup. Its camera sees the cup. Its brain decides to grab it. Its arm motors need to move. Explanation: Without ROS 2, each part works alone. The camera can't tell the brain what it sees. The brain can't tell the arm what to do. ROS 2 connects everything. The camera publishes what it sees. The brain processes this data. It sends commands to the arm. All of this happens automatically. Takeaway: ROS 2 is the communication network that makes robots work as a unified system.

You might wonder why we use ROS 2 instead of building from scratch. Reusability: Thousands of developers have built ROS 2 tools. You can use their work instead of starting over. Industry Standard: Most robot companies use ROS 2. Learning it opens career opportunities. Hardware Support: ROS 2 works with many robots. You write code once. It runs on different hardware. Active Community: When you have problems, thousands of developers can help.
This module covers five main topics:
Learn about nodes, topics, services, and actions. These are the building blocks of robot programs.
Build ROS 2 programs using Python. Python is easier than C++ for beginners.
Define robot models using URDF and Xacro. These formats describe robot structure.
Create, build, and launch ROS 2 packages. Packages organize your code.
Build a real project. Make a humanoid robot walk using joint control.

By the end of this module, you will be able to: Understand how ROS 2 programs communicate Create nodes, topics, services, and actions Write robot programs in Python Define robot models Build and launch packages Control humanoid robot walking

A node is a single program. It does one specific job. Nodes are the fundamental units in ROS 2. Think of nodes as workers in a factory. Each worker has one job. They work together. The factory runs smoothly.

Single Purpose: Each node should do one thing well. Don't create a node that does everything. Examples of good nodes: Camera driver (publishes images) Object detector (finds objects in images) Motor controller (moves robot joints) Bad node example: One node that handles camera, detects objects, AND moves motors

You might wonder why not put everything in one program. Modularity: You can replace one node. You don't change others. Switch cameras? Just replace the camera node. Parallel Processing: Multiple nodes run at the same time. Your robot can see, think, and move at once. Fault Isolation: If one node crashes, others keep running. The robot keeps working.

Type: Analogy Context: Imagine a restaurant kitchen. You have chefs. You have waiters. You have customers. They need to communicate. Explanation: Each person is like a node. The chef cooks. The waiter serves. The cashier handles payment. Each does one job well. If the chef leaves, a new chef can replace them. The waiter doesn't change. The restaurant keeps running. Takeaway: Nodes provide modularity. Each component is independent. The system is robust.

Here's the simplest possible node: simple_node.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node class SimpleNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('simple_node') self.get_logger().info('Simple node is running!') def main(): rclpy.init() node = SimpleNode() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() This node doesn't do much. It just logs a message. But it's complete and runnable.

Line by line: import rclpy - Import the ROS 2 Python client library from rclpy.node import Node - Import the base Node class class SimpleNode(Node) - Create our node class super().__init__('simple_node') - Initialize with a name self.get_logger().info(...) - Log a message rclpy.init() - Initialize the ROS 2 system rclpy.spin(node) - Keep the node running node.destroy_node() - Clean up rclpy.shutdown() - Shut down ROS 2
Save the file. Then run it: python3 simple_node.py You'll see: [INFO] [simple_node]: Simple node is running! The node runs. It stays alive. Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

Every node needs a unique name. This name identifies it in the ROS 2 system. super().__init__('simple_node') # Name is 'simple_node' Naming rules: Use lowercase letters Use underscores for spaces Make names descriptive Avoid special characters Good names: camera_driver, object_detector, motor_controller Bad names: node1, MyNode, n

A node has a lifecycle: Initialize: rclpy.init() sets up ROS 2 Create: SimpleNode() creates the node Spin: rclpy.spin() keeps it running Destroy: destroy_node() cleans up Shutdown: rclpy.shutdown() stops ROS 2 Always follow this pattern. It ensures proper cleanup.

Type: Scenario Context: Your humanoid robot starts up. Multiple nodes need to initialize. Explanation: The robot boots. First, the camera node initializes. Then the IMU node. Then the motor controller. Each follows the same lifecycle. Initialize. Create. Spin. If you power down, each calls destroy and shutdown. This ensures clean exits. No corrupted data. No stuck processes. Takeaway: Following the lifecycle pattern ensures reliable robot operation.
documents.s: Example 2: Node Lifecycle in Real Robots

documents.t: You can list all running nodes: ros2 node list This shows all active nodes in your system. For detailed information about a specific node: ros2 node info /simple_node This displays: Subscribers Publishers Services Actions

# Wrong - node exits immediately def main(): rclpy.init() node = SimpleNode() # Missing: rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() The node starts. Then it exits immediately. You must call spin() to keep it alive.

# Wrong - no cleanup def main(): rclpy.init() node = SimpleNode() rclpy.spin(node) # Missing: destroy_node() and shutdown() Always clean up. Call destroy_node(). Call shutdown(). This prevents resource leaks.
Running two nodes with the same name causes conflicts. Each node needs a unique name.

Nodes are independent programs that do one specific job Each node has a unique name Nodes follow a lifecycle: init, create, spin, destroy, shutdown Multiple nodes enable modularity, parallelism, and fault isolation Keep nodes simple and focused

Topics are for continuous data streams. Think sensor data, robot state, or camera images. Topics use the publisher-subscriber pattern. Publishers send data. Subscribers receive data. They don't know about each other.
Publishers send data to a topic. Subscribers receive data from a topic. Many publishers can write to one topic. Many subscribers can read from it. They are independent.

Think of a topic as a message board in an office. Anyone can post messages (publishers) Anyone can read messages (subscribers) Posters don't know who reads Readers don't know who posts Multiple people can post or read simultaneously

Use topics for: Sensor data (camera images, laser scans) Robot state (joint positions, velocities) Continuous monitoring (battery level, temperature) Don't use topics for: Requests that need replies (use services) Long tasks that need feedback (use actions)

Here's a node that publishes temperature data: temperature_publisher.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import Float32 class TemperaturePublisher(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('temperature_publisher') # Create publisher self.publisher = self.create_publisher(Float32, 'temperature', 10) # Publish every 1 second self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.publish_temperature) self.temperature = 25.0 def publish_temperature(self): msg = Float32() msg.data = self.temperature self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Publishing: {msg.data}°C') # Simulate temperature change self.temperature += 0.1 def main(): rclpy.init() node = TemperaturePublisher() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Key lines: self.create_publisher(Float32, 'temperature', 10) - Create a publisher Float32: Message type 'temperature': Topic name 10: Queue size (how many messages to buffer) self.create_timer(1.0, self.publish_temperature) - Create a timer 1.0: Interval in seconds self.publish_temperature: Callback function self.publisher.publish(msg) - Publish the message

Here's a node that subscribes to temperature data: temperature_subscriber.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import Float32 class TemperatureSubscriber(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('temperature_subscriber') # Create subscriber self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Float32, 'temperature', self.temperature_callback, 10 ) def temperature_callback(self, msg): self.get_logger().info(f'Received: {msg.data}°C') # React to high temperature if msg.data > 30.0: self.get_logger().warn('Temperature is too high!') def main(): rclpy.init() node = TemperatureSubscriber() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Key lines: self.create_subscription(...) - Create a subscriber Float32: Message type (must match publisher) 'temperature': Topic name (must match publisher) self.temperature_callback: Function to call when data arrives 10: Queue size def temperature_callback(self, msg) - Callback function Called automatically when new data arrives msg: The received message

Terminal 1 - Start the publisher: python3 temperature_publisher.py Output: [INFO] [temperature_publisher]: Publishing: 25.0°C [INFO] [temperature_publisher]: Publishing: 25.1°C [INFO] [temperature_publisher]: Publishing: 25.2°C Terminal 2 - Start the subscriber: python3 temperature_subscriber.py Output: [INFO] [temperature_subscriber]: Received: 25.3°C [INFO] [temperature_subscriber]: Received: 25.4°C [INFO] [temperature_subscriber]: Received: 25.5°C They communicate! The publisher sends. The subscriber receives.

Type: Scenario Context: You have a robot with multiple temperature sensors. You want to log all temperatures and sound an alarm if any gets too hot. Explanation: Create one publisher node per sensor. Each publishes to the temperature topic. Create one subscriber node. It monitors the topic. It receives data from all sensors. The sensors don't know about the monitor. The monitor doesn't know how many sensors exist. This is loose coupling. You can add sensors. You can remove sensors. No code changes needed. Takeaway: Topics enable flexible, scalable communication. Nodes remain independent.

List all active topics: ros2 topic list See topic details: ros2 topic info /temperature Output shows: Message type Number of publishers Number of subscribers Echo topic data in real-time: ros2 topic echo /temperature This prints all messages as they arrive.

Topics use typed messages. Common types: std_msgs/Float32 - Single floating point number std_msgs/String - Text string std_msgs/Int32 - Integer sensor_msgs/Image - Camera image geometry_msgs/Twist - Velocity command Import from the appropriate package: from std_msgs.msg import Float32 from sensor_msgs.msg import Image from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist

The queue size (10 in our examples) is part of QoS settings. Queue Size: Small (10): For fast-changing data Large (100): For important data you can't lose QoS profiles control: Reliability (best effort vs. reliable) Durability (volatile vs. transient local) History (keep last vs. keep all) Default settings work for most cases. Advanced users can customize.

# Publisher uses Float32 self.publisher = self.create_publisher(Float32, 'temperature', 10) # Subscriber uses Int32 - WRONG! self.subscription = self.create_subscription(Int32, 'temperature', ...) Message types must match exactly.

def temperature_callback(self, msg): # Don't do this - blocks for 10 seconds! time.sleep(10) self.get_logger().info(f'Received: {msg.data}') Keep callbacks short. Long operations block other callbacks.

# Wrong - subscription gets garbage collected def __init__(self): self.create_subscription(Float32, 'temperature', self.callback, 10) Always store the subscription: # Correct def __init__(self): self.subscription = self.create_subscription(...)

Topics enable publisher-subscriber communication Publishers send data without knowing subscribers Subscribers receive data without knowing publishers Message types must match between publisher and subscriber Use topics for continuous data streams Keep callbacks short and non-blocking

Services are for one-time requests that need a reply. Think "what's your battery level?" or "add these two numbers." Services use synchronous request-response. The client sends a request. The server processes it. The client waits. The server sends a response.

Service Server waits for requests. When one arrives, it processes it. Then it sends a response. Service Client sends a request. It waits for the response. Unlike topics, services are synchronous. The client must wait for the answer.

Type: Analogy Context: You finish eating at a restaurant. You need to pay. Explanation: You ask the waiter for the bill. This is your request. The waiter goes to the cashier. The cashier calculates your total. This takes time. You wait. The waiter returns with the bill. This is the response. You needed an answer. You got it. Takeaway: Services provide request-response communication. Clients get answers.

Use services for: Queries (get current state) Commands that complete quickly (turn on LED) Calculations (inverse kinematics) Don't use services for: Long-running tasks (use actions instead) Continuous data streams (use topics instead) Rule of thumb: If it takes more than 1 second, use an action. Not a service.

Here's a service that adds two integers: add_two_ints_server.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts class AddTwoIntsServer(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('add_two_ints_server') # Create service self.srv = self.create_service( AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints', self.add_two_ints_callback ) self.get_logger().info('Add Two Ints Server ready') def add_two_ints_callback(self, request, response): response.sum = request.a + request.b self.get_logger().info(f'Request: {request.a} + {request.b} = {response.sum}') return response def main(): rclpy.init() node = AddTwoIntsServer() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Key lines: from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts - Import service type Service types end in .srv Located in service packages self.create_service(...) - Create a service server AddTwoInts: Service type 'add_two_ints': Service name self.add_two_ints_callback: Handler function def add_two_ints_callback(self, request, response) - Service callback request: Contains client's request data response: Object to fill with response data Must return response response.sum = request.a + request.b - Process the request Access request fields: request.a, request.b Set response fields: response.sum

Here's a client that calls the service: add_two_ints_client.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts class AddTwoIntsClient(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('add_two_ints_client') # Create client self.client = self.create_client(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints') # Wait for service to be available while not self.client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0): self.get_logger().info('Waiting for service...') self.get_logger().info('Service available') def send_request(self, a, b): request = AddTwoInts.Request() request.a = a request.b = b # Send request future = self.client.call_async(request) return future def main(): rclpy.init() node = AddTwoIntsClient() # Send request future = node.send_request(5, 7) # Wait for response rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, future) if future.result() is not None: result = future.result() node.get_logger().info(f'Result: {result.sum}') else: node.get_logger().error('Service call failed') node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Key lines: self.create_client(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints') - Create a client Service type and name must match server self.client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0) - Wait for server Returns True when server is available Timeout prevents infinite waiting request = AddTwoInts.Request() - Create request object Set request fields: request.a, request.b future = self.client.call_async(request) - Call service asynchronously Returns a Future object Non-blocking call rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, future) - Wait for response Blocks until service returns future.result() - Get the response Contains server's response data

Terminal 1 - Start the server: python3 add_two_ints_server.py Output: [INFO] [add_two_ints_server]: Add Two Ints Server ready Terminal 2 - Run the client: python3 add_two_ints_client.py Output: [INFO] [add_two_ints_client]: Service available [INFO] [add_two_ints_client]: Result: 12 Server output: [INFO] [add_two_ints_server]: Request: 5 + 7 = 12 They communicate! The client requests. The server responds.

List all available services: ros2 service list See service details: ros2 service type /add_two_ints Call a service from command line: ros2 service call /add_two_ints example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts "{a: 3, b: 4}" Output: sum: 7

Services have defined types with request and response structures. Common service types: example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts - Add two integers std_srvs/srv/SetBool - Set a boolean value std_srvs/srv/Trigger - Trigger an action View service type definition: ros2 interface show example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts Output shows request and response fields: int64 a int64 b --- int64 sum The --- separates request (above) from response (below).

Synchronous (blocking): # Not shown in examples - blocks the entire node response = client.call(request) # Waits here This blocks everything. Don't use in production. Asynchronous (non-blocking): # Our example uses this future = client.call_async(request) # Returns immediately rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, future) # Wait separately response = future.result() This allows other operations while waiting.

# Wrong - service might not exist yet client = self.create_client(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints') future = client.call_async(request) # May fail! Always wait: # Correct while not client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0): self.get_logger().info('Waiting...')

# Wrong - doesn't return response def callback(self, request, response): response.sum = request.a + request.b # Missing: return response Always return the response: # Correct def callback(self, request, response): response.sum = request.a + request.b return response
# Bad - service blocks for 60 seconds def callback(self, request, response): time.sleep(60) # Don't do this! return response If it takes more than 1 second, use an action instead.
documents.s: Mistake 3: Using Services for Long Tasks

documents.t: Services provide synchronous request-response communication Service servers wait for requests and send responses Service clients send requests and wait for responses Use services for quick queries and commands (< 1 second) Always wait for service availability before calling Use asynchronous calls to avoid blocking

Actions are for tasks that take time and need feedback. Think "navigate to the kitchen" or "pick up the cup." Actions combine the best of topics and services. They provide feedback during execution. You can cancel them if needed.

Action Server performs the long-running task. It sends feedback updates. Action Client sends a goal. It receives feedback. It can cancel if needed. Unlike services, actions don't block. The client stays responsive.

Type: Analogy Context: You order food at a restaurant. It takes 20 minutes to prepare. Explanation: You place your order. This is the goal. The kitchen starts cooking. Every 5 minutes, the waiter updates you: "Your order is 25% done." This is feedback. You stay at your table. You can talk. You can cancel the order if you change your mind. After 20 minutes, your food arrives. This is the result. Takeaway: Actions provide feedback during long operations. Clients stay responsive. Cancellation is possible.

Use actions for: Navigation (takes seconds or minutes) Manipulation (pick and place) Any task where you want progress updates Don't use actions for: Quick requests (use services) Continuous streams (use topics) Rule of thumb: If it takes more than 1 second AND you want progress updates, use an action.

Actions have three parts: Goal: What you want to achieve Feedback: Progress updates during execution Result: Final outcome when done This is more powerful than services. Services only have request and result.

Services block while waiting. If navigation takes 2 minutes, your client is stuck. You can't cancel. You don't get updates. Actions solve this. The client stays responsive. It gets updates. It can cancel.

Type: Comparison Context: You want your robot to navigate to a target position 10 meters away. Explanation: With a service: Send navigation request Wait 2 minutes (blocked) Get result No progress updates Can't cancel If robot gets stuck, you wait 2 minutes to find out With an action: Send navigation goal Receive feedback every second: "3m traveled", "5m traveled", "7m traveled" Client stays responsive Can cancel anytime Know immediately if robot is stuck Takeaway: Actions are essential for long tasks. They provide visibility and control.
Here's what a simple action looks like:

# Goal int32 order --- # Result int32[] sequence --- # Feedback int32[] partial_sequence Three sections separated by ---: Goal: What the client wants Result: What the server returns when done Feedback: Progress updates during execution

Here's the concept (simplified for clarity): # Conceptual action server structure class FibonacciActionServer(Node): def execute_callback(self, goal_handle): # 1. Extract goal order = goal_handle.request.order # 2. Initialize feedback feedback = Fibonacci.Feedback() # 3. Process goal and send periodic feedback sequence = [0, 1] for i in range(1, order): # Calculate next number sequence.append(sequence[i] + sequence[i-1]) # Send feedback feedback.partial_sequence = sequence goal_handle.publish_feedback(feedback) # Simulate work time.sleep(1) # 4. Send final result result = Fibonacci.Result() result.sequence = sequence goal_handle.succeed() return result Key concepts: execute_callback: Main function that processes the goal goal_handle.publish_feedback(): Send progress updates goal_handle.succeed(): Mark goal as complete return result: Final outcome

Here's the concept (simplified): # Conceptual action client structure class FibonacciActionClient(Node): def send_goal(self, order): # 1. Create goal goal = Fibonacci.Goal() goal.order = order # 2. Send goal asynchronously send_goal_future = self.client.send_goal_async( goal, feedback_callback=self.feedback_callback ) # 3. Wait for goal acceptance goal_handle = await send_goal_future # 4. Wait for result result_future = goal_handle.get_result_async() result = await result_future return result.result def feedback_callback(self, feedback): # Called automatically when feedback arrives print(f'Progress: {feedback.feedback.partial_sequence}') Key concepts: send_goal_async(): Send goal without blocking feedback_callback: Receives progress updates get_result_async(): Wait for final result Callbacks keep client responsive

Actions progress through states: Pending: Goal sent, waiting for server to accept Active: Server is working on the goal Succeeded: Goal completed successfully Aborted: Server stopped due to error Canceled: Client canceled the goal You can check state and respond accordingly.

Clients can cancel goals: # Send goal goal_handle = await client.send_goal_async(goal) # Later, cancel it cancel_future = goal_handle.cancel_goal_async() The server handles cancellation gracefully. It stops processing. Returns a canceled state.

List all available actions: ros2 action list See action details: ros2 action info /fibonacci Send a goal from command line: ros2 action send_goal /fibonacci example_interfaces/action/Fibonacci "{order: 5}" You'll see feedback updates and final result.

Type: Scenario Context: Your humanoid robot needs to walk 5 meters forward. Explanation: You send a walking action goal: "Walk 5 meters." The robot starts walking. Every second, it sends feedback: "0.5m walked", "1.0m walked", "1.5m walked". You see progress in real-time. If the robot trips at 2 meters, you get feedback immediately. You can cancel the walk. You can send a new goal. The robot is responsive. Without actions, you'd send a command and wait blindly for 20 seconds. Takeaway: Actions make robots controllable and observable during long tasks.

Here's a decision guide: Use Topics when: Data flows continuously You don't need confirmation Multiple listeners might exist Example: Sensor data, robot state Use Services when: You need a reply The task is quick (< 1 second) It's a one-time request Example: Get current position, calculate something Use Actions when: The task takes time (> 1 second) You want progress updates You might need to cancel Example: Navigation, manipulation, long computations
# Bad - action overhead for 0.1 second task action = client.send_goal(turn_led_on) Use a service instead. Actions add complexity.
documents.s: Mistake 1: Using Actions for Quick Tasks

documents.t: # Bad - ignores feedback goal_handle = client.send_goal_async(goal) # No feedback callback registered Always register a feedback callback. Otherwise, why use actions?
# Bad - defeats the purpose of actions result = client.send_goal(goal) # Synchronous - blocks everything Use asynchronous calls. Keep your client responsive.

Actions enable long-running tasks with feedback and cancellation Action servers process goals and send feedback Action clients stay responsive while receiving updates Actions have three parts: goal, result, and feedback Use actions when tasks take >1 second and need progress visibility Clients can cancel actions at any time

We follow these conventions: Classes: PascalCase (e.g., TemperaturePublisher) Functions: snake_case (e.g., publish_temperature) Node names: lowercase with underscores (e.g., 'temperature_publisher') Topic names: lowercase with slashes (e.g., '/sensors/temperature')

rclpy is the Python library for ROS 2. The name comes from "ROS Client Library Python." This subtopic teaches you the fundamentals. Node initialization. Lifecycle management. Best practices. Master these patterns. They form the foundation of all Python ROS 2 development.
rclpy provides Python APIs for: Creating nodes Publishing and subscribing to topics Creating services Handling actions Managing parameters Think of it as your Python toolkit for robotics.

Type: Comparison Context: You might wonder why use Python instead of C++. C++ is faster, right? Explanation: Python is easier to learn and write. For most robot tasks, Python is fast enough. You can prototype quickly. You can test ideas in minutes instead of hours. When you need speed later, you can optimize specific parts in C++. But start with Python to learn concepts. Takeaway: Python lets you focus on robot logic instead of fighting with syntax.

Every rclpy program follows the same pattern: 1. Initialize ROS 2 → rclpy.init() 2. Create node → Node() 3. Spin (run node) → rclpy.spin() 4. Destroy node → node.destroy_node() 5. Shutdown ROS 2 → rclpy.shutdown() This lifecycle ensures proper setup and cleanup.

Let's create a simple node: hello_node.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node class HelloNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('hello_node') self.get_logger().info('Hello, Robot World!') def main(args=None): rclpy.init(args=args) node = HelloNode() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Line by line: import rclpy - Import the ROS 2 Python library from rclpy.node import Node - Import the base Node class class HelloNode(Node) - Create your custom node class super().__init__('hello_node') - Call parent constructor with node name self.get_logger().info(...) - Log a message rclpy.init(args=args) - Initialize ROS 2 system node = HelloNode() - Create an instance of your node rclpy.spin(node) - Keep the node running (blocks here) node.destroy_node() - Clean up node resources rclpy.shutdown() - Shutdown ROS 2 system
Save the file. Then run it: python3 hello_node.py Output: [INFO] [hello_node]: Hello, Robot World! The node runs and stays alive. Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

This function initializes the ROS 2 system. rclpy.init(args=args) What it does: Sets up the ROS 2 context Parses command-line arguments Initializes logging Prepares communication infrastructure When to call it: Once at program start, before creating any nodes. Arguments: Pass command-line args to enable ROS 2 remapping: python3 hello_node.py --ros-args --remap __node:=my_node This remaps the node name at runtime.

This function keeps your node running. rclpy.spin(node) What it does: Processes callbacks (timers, subscriptions, services) Handles ROS 2 communication Blocks until Ctrl+C or shutdown Why it's needed: Without spin, your node would exit immediately after __init__.

Type: Scenario Context: You forget to call rclpy.spin(). Explanation: def main(): rclpy.init() node = HelloNode() # Missing: rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() The program runs. It prints "Hello, Robot World!". Then it exits immediately. No time for callbacks. No time for subscriptions. The node dies before it can do anything useful. Takeaway: Always call spin() to keep your node alive.

Cleanup is important. It prevents resource leaks. node.destroy_node() # Clean up node resources rclpy.shutdown() # Shutdown ROS 2 system destroy_node(): Destroys publishers, subscribers, timers Releases network resources Called on the specific node instance shutdown(): Shuts down entire ROS 2 system Stops all communication Called once at program end Order matters: Destroy nodes before shutdown.

Every node needs a unique name: super().__init__('hello_node') # Name is 'hello_node' Naming conventions: Use lowercase letters Use underscores for spaces Make names descriptive Avoid special characters Good names: camera_driver, object_detector, motor_controller Bad names: node1, MyNode, n
Verify your node is running: ros2 node list Output: /hello_node Get detailed node information: ros2 node info /hello_node Shows subscribers, publishers, services, and actions.

Use the logger for output instead of print(): self.get_logger().info('Information message') self.get_logger().warn('Warning message') self.get_logger().error('Error message') self.get_logger().debug('Debug message') Why use logger instead of print(): Timestamps included automatically Node name added to messages Log levels allow filtering Integration with ROS 2 logging system

From least to most severe: DEBUG: Detailed diagnostic information INFO: General information WARN: Something unexpected but not critical ERROR: A serious problem occurred FATAL: Critical failure, node cannot continue

You can use Python context managers for cleaner code: hello_node_context.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node class HelloNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('hello_node') self.get_logger().info('Hello, Robot World!') def main(args=None): with rclpy.init(args=args): node = HelloNode() try: rclpy.spin(node) finally: node.destroy_node() if __name__ == '__main__': main() The with statement ensures automatic cleanup. Even if exceptions occur. Note: This is advanced. Stick with the standard pattern when starting out.

Handle shutdown signals properly: import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node def main(args=None): rclpy.init(args=args) node = HelloNode() try: rclpy.spin(node) except KeyboardInterrupt: pass # Ctrl+C pressed finally: node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() This catches Ctrl+C and ensures cleanup runs.
# Wrong - rclpy not initialized def main(): # Missing: rclpy.init() node = HelloNode() # Error! Always call rclpy.init() first.
# Wrong - multiple init calls def main(): rclpy.init() rclpy.init() # Error! Already initialized Call init() only once per program.

# Wrong - parent constructor not called class HelloNode(Node): def __init__(self): # Missing: super().__init__('hello_node') self.get_logger().info('Hello') # Error! Logger doesn't exist Always call super().__init__(node_name) first.
# Wrong order def main(): rclpy.init() node = HelloNode() rclpy.spin(node) rclpy.shutdown() # Wrong! Shutdown before destroy node.destroy_node() # Too late Correct order: destroy node, then shutdown.

try: rclpy.spin(node) except KeyboardInterrupt: self.get_logger().info('Shutting down gracefully') except Exception as e: self.get_logger().error(f'Unexpected error: {e}') finally: node.destroy_node()
Always use the same lifecycle pattern: rclpy.init() node = MyNode() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown()

rclpy is the Python library for ROS 2 development Every node follows the init → create → spin → destroy → shutdown lifecycle rclpy.init() initializes ROS 2 (call once) rclpy.spin() keeps the node running (blocks) destroy_node() and shutdown() clean up resources Use the logger instead of print() for output Always handle Ctrl+C gracefully
