Publishers send data to topics. You learned the concept in Chapter 1. Now learn the implementation. This subtopic shows you how to create publishers in Python. You'll learn message types. Publishing rates. Quality of Service settings.

Use create_publisher() to make a publisher: self.publisher = self.create_publisher(MessageType, 'topic_name', queue_size) Parameters: MessageType: The type of message to publish 'topic_name': The topic to publish to queue_size: How many messages to buffer (usually 10)

simple_publisher.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import String class SimplePublisher(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('simple_publisher') self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'robot_status', 10) self.get_logger().info('Publisher created') def publish_message(self, text): msg = String() msg.data = text self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Published: {text}') def main(): rclpy.init() node = SimplePublisher() node.publish_message('Hello from publisher!') rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() This publishes one message and exits.

Most publishers send data repeatedly. Use timers: periodic_publisher.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import String class PeriodicPublisher(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('periodic_publisher') # Create publisher self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'robot_status', 10) # Create timer (publishes every 1 second) self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback) self.counter = 0 def timer_callback(self): msg = String() msg.data = f'Message {self.counter}' self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Published: {msg.data}') self.counter += 1 def main(): rclpy.init() node = PeriodicPublisher() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Key lines: self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback) - Create a timer 1.0: Period in seconds self.timer_callback: Function to call def timer_callback(self) - Called every second Creates message Publishes message Increments counter self.publisher.publish(msg) - Send the message The timer automatically calls your callback. No manual loops needed.

Basic types: from std_msgs.msg import String, Int32, Float32, Bool # String message msg = String() msg.data = "Hello" # Integer message msg = Int32() msg.data = 42 # Float message msg = Float32() msg.data = 3.14 # Boolean message msg = Bool() msg.data = True

For positions, velocities, poses: from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist, Point, Pose # Velocity command msg = Twist() msg.linear.x = 1.0 # Forward velocity msg.angular.z = 0.5 # Rotation velocity # Point in 3D space msg = Point() msg.x = 1.0 msg.y = 2.0 msg.z = 3.0
For sensor data: from sensor_msgs.msg import Image, LaserScan, Imu # Messages are more complex # Usually filled by sensor drivers

Let's create a temperature sensor publisher: temperature_publisher.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import Float32 import random class TemperaturePublisher(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('temperature_publisher') # Create publisher self.publisher = self.create_publisher( Float32, '/sensors/temperature', 10 ) # Publish every 0.5 seconds (2 Hz) self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.publish_temperature) self.temperature = 25.0 def publish_temperature(self): # Simulate temperature sensor noise = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) self.temperature += noise # Create and publish message msg = Float32() msg.data = self.temperature self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Temperature: {self.temperature:.2f}°C') def main(): rclpy.init() node = TemperaturePublisher() try: rclpy.spin(node) except KeyboardInterrupt: pass finally: node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Type: Scenario Context: You have a robot with a temperature sensor. You want to publish readings for other nodes to use. Explanation: This publisher simulates a real temperature sensor. It publishes at 2 Hz (twice per second). Other nodes can subscribe to /sensors/temperature and react. Maybe one node logs the data. Another node activates cooling if temperature is too high. The publisher doesn't know or care who subscribes. It just sends data reliably. Takeaway: Publishers provide data independence. Nodes remain decoupled.

Choose appropriate rates: Fast (10-100 Hz): Camera images IMU data Joint states Medium (1-10 Hz): Temperature sensors Battery status GPS position Slow (0.1-1 Hz): System diagnostics Heartbeat messages Slow-changing state Trade-off: Higher rates consume more bandwidth and CPU.

The queue size parameter controls buffering: self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', 10) # ^^ # queue size Small queue (10): For fast-changing data Old data becomes stale quickly Example: Camera images Large queue (100+): For important data you can't lose Data stays relevant longer Example: Commands, diagnostics Default: Use 10 for most cases.

QoS controls message delivery guarantees: from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, ReliabilityPolicy, DurabilityPolicy # Create custom QoS qos = QoSProfile( depth=10, reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE, durability=DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL ) # Use custom QoS self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', qos) Reliability: RELIABLE: Guarantees delivery (like TCP) BEST_EFFORT: May lose messages (like UDP, faster) Durability: VOLATILE: Only send to current subscribers TRANSIENT_LOCAL: Send to late-joining subscribers Default QoS works for most cases. Customize only when needed.

Verify your publisher is working: # List all topics ros2 topic list # See topic details ros2 topic info /sensors/temperature # Echo messages in real-time ros2 topic echo /sensors/temperature # Check publishing rate ros2 topic hz /sensors/temperature

You can create multiple publishers: class MultiPublisher(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('multi_publisher') # Publisher 1 self.temp_pub = self.create_publisher( Float32, '/sensors/temperature', 10) # Publisher 2 self.battery_pub = self.create_publisher( Float32, '/sensors/battery', 10) # Different timer for each self.timer1 = self.create_timer(1.0, self.publish_temp) self.timer2 = self.create_timer(5.0, self.publish_battery) def publish_temp(self): msg = Float32() msg.data = 25.0 self.temp_pub.publish(msg) def publish_battery(self): msg = Float32() msg.data = 12.5 self.battery_pub.publish(msg) Each publisher can have its own rate.

# Wrong - publisher gets garbage collected def __init__(self): self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', 10) # Lost! Always store the publisher: # Correct def __init__(self): self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', 10)

# May not work - subscriber not ready yet def __init__(self): self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', 10) msg = String() msg.data = "Hello" self.publisher.publish(msg) # Too fast! Solution: Use timers or wait for subscribers: # Better - wait for subscribers while self.publisher.get_subscription_count() == 0: time.sleep(0.1) self.publisher.publish(msg) Or use TRANSIENT_LOCAL QoS to store messages for late subscribers.

# Bad - message reused, causes issues self.msg = String() def timer_callback(self): self.msg.data = "Hello" self.publisher.publish(self.msg) Create fresh messages in callback: # Good - new message each time def timer_callback(self): msg = String() msg.data = "Hello" self.publisher.publish(msg)
# Temperature doesn't change fast - 1 Hz is fine self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.callback) # IMU data changes fast - 100 Hz needed self.timer = self.create_timer(0.01, self.callback)
def timer_callback(self): msg = Float32() msg.data = 25.0 self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Published: {msg.data}') # Good!

Use create_publisher() to create publishers Use create_timer() for periodic publishing Message types come from packages like std_msgs, geometry_msgs Queue size controls message buffering (default: 10) Publishing rate should match data update rate Always store the publisher reference Create new message instances in callbacks

You can send data with publishers. Next, learn how to receive data with subscribers. Continue to: 2.3 Subscribers - Receiving Data Related topics: 1.2 Topics 2.1 rclpy Basics Chapter 2 Overview Try it yourself: Create a publisher that sends your name every 2 seconds Create a publisher that sends random numbers Use ros2 topic echo to verify your messages Experiment with different publishing rates
Estimated Reading Time: 8 minutes Prerequisites: 2.1 rclpy Basics, 2.2 Publishers Difficulty: Beginner

Subscribers receive data from topics. You learned the concept in Chapter 1. Now learn the implementation. This subtopic shows you how to create subscribers in Python. You'll learn callback patterns. Message handling. Efficient data processing.

Use create_subscription() to make a subscriber: self.subscription = self.create_subscription( MessageType, 'topic_name', callback_function, queue_size ) Parameters: MessageType: The type of message to receive 'topic_name': The topic to subscribe to callback_function: Function to call when message arrives queue_size: How many messages to buffer (usually 10)

simple_subscriber.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import String class SimpleSubscriber(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('simple_subscriber') self.subscription = self.create_subscription( String, 'robot_status', self.listener_callback, 10 ) self.get_logger().info('Subscriber ready') def listener_callback(self, msg): self.get_logger().info(f'Received: {msg.data}') def main(): rclpy.init() node = SimpleSubscriber() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Key lines: self.create_subscription(...) - Create subscriber Must match publisher's message type Must match publisher's topic name self.listener_callback - Pass function reference Don't call it (listener_callback()) Just pass the name (listener_callback) def listener_callback(self, msg) - Callback function Called automatically when data arrives msg: The received message Access message data via msg.data, msg.x, etc.

Terminal 1 - Run subscriber: python3 simple_subscriber.py Output: [INFO] [simple_subscriber]: Subscriber ready Terminal 2 - Publish a message: ros2 topic pub /robot_status std_msgs/msg/String "data: 'Hello from command line'" Subscriber output: [INFO] [simple_subscriber]: Received: Hello from command line The subscriber receives and processes the message!

Let's create a subscriber that monitors temperature: temperature_subscriber.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import Float32 class TemperatureSubscriber(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('temperature_subscriber') self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Float32, '/sensors/temperature', self.temperature_callback, 10 ) self.high_temp_threshold = 30.0 def temperature_callback(self, msg): temp = msg.data self.get_logger().info(f'Temperature: {temp:.2f}°C') # React to high temperature if temp > self.high_temp_threshold: self.get_logger().warn( f'High temperature alert: {temp:.2f}°C!' ) def main(): rclpy.init() node = TemperatureSubscriber() try: rclpy.spin(node) except KeyboardInterrupt: pass finally: node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() This subscriber monitors temperature and warns when it's too high.

Type: Scenario Context: Your robot has a temperature sensor publishing data. You need to monitor it and take action if it overheats. Explanation: The subscriber receives every temperature reading. It logs the value. It checks against a threshold. If temperature exceeds 30°C, it warns. You could extend this to trigger cooling, slow down motors, or send alerts. The subscriber reacts to data without knowing the publisher. Takeaway: Subscribers enable reactive behavior based on incoming data.

Callbacks execute automatically when messages arrive: 1. Message published 2. ROS 2 delivers to subscriber 3. Your callback function executes 4. Callback returns 5. Wait for next message Important: Keep callbacks short and fast.

You can process, filter, or transform data: class DataProcessor(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('data_processor') self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Float32, '/raw_sensor', self.process_callback, 10 ) self.values = [] def process_callback(self, msg): # Store value self.values.append(msg.data) # Keep only last 10 values if len(self.values) > 10: self.values.pop(0) # Calculate moving average average = sum(self.values) / len(self.values) self.get_logger().info( f'Raw: {msg.data:.2f}, Average: {average:.2f}' ) This implements a moving average filter.

Nodes often both subscribe and publish: data_filter_node.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import Float32 class DataFilter(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('data_filter') # Subscribe to raw data self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Float32, '/sensors/temperature_raw', self.filter_callback, 10 ) # Publish filtered data self.publisher = self.create_publisher( Float32, '/sensors/temperature_filtered', 10 ) self.previous_value = None def filter_callback(self, msg): current = msg.data # Simple spike filter if self.previous_value is not None: diff = abs(current - self.previous_value) # Reject large spikes if diff > 5.0: self.get_logger().warn(f'Spike detected: {diff:.2f}') return # Don't publish # Accept value self.previous_value = current # Publish filtered value filtered_msg = Float32() filtered_msg.data = current self.publisher.publish(filtered_msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Filtered: {current:.2f}°C') def main(): rclpy.init() node = DataFilter() try: rclpy.spin(node) except KeyboardInterrupt: pass finally: node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() This creates a data processing pipeline.

Type: Pattern Context: You have noisy sensor data. You need to clean it before using it. Explanation: Create a chain of nodes. The sensor publishes raw data. A filter node subscribes to raw data and publishes filtered data. Control nodes subscribe to filtered data. Each node has one job. The pipeline is modular. You can swap filters easily. You can add more processing steps. Takeaway: Subscriber + publisher nodes create data processing pipelines.

Verify your subscriber is working: # List all topics ros2 topic list # See who subscribes to a topic ros2 topic info /sensors/temperature # Check if subscriber is receiving # (subscriber should log messages)

Subscriber QoS must be compatible with publisher QoS: from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, ReliabilityPolicy # Create QoS matching publisher qos = QoSProfile( depth=10, reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE ) # Use with subscriber self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Float32, 'topic', self.callback, qos # Use QoS instead of simple queue size ) Rule: If publisher uses RELIABLE, subscriber should too.

# Wrong - subscription gets garbage collected def __init__(self): self.create_subscription(String, 'topic', self.callback, 10) Always store it: # Correct def __init__(self): self.subscription = self.create_subscription(...)

# Bad - blocks for 10 seconds def callback(self, msg): time.sleep(10) # Don't do this! self.get_logger().info(f'Received: {msg.data}') Keep callbacks fast: # Good - quick processing def callback(self, msg): self.get_logger().info(f'Received: {msg.data}') # If you need slow processing, use a separate thread or timer

# Wrong - don't call callback yourself def __init__(self): self.subscription = self.create_subscription(...) msg = String() msg.data = "Test" self.listener_callback(msg) # Bad! Let ROS 2 call the callback. Don't call it manually.

# Publisher uses Float32 publisher = self.create_publisher(Float32, 'topic', 10) # Subscriber uses Int32 - WRONG! subscription = self.create_subscription(Int32, 'topic', callback, 10) Message types must match exactly.
# Good - quick processing def callback(self, msg): self.latest_value = msg.data self.get_logger().info(f'Received: {msg.data}')

# Bad - heavy computation in callback def callback(self, msg): result = expensive_function(msg.data) # Blocks! # Better - store and process later def callback(self, msg): self.queue.append(msg.data) def timer_callback(self): if self.queue: result = expensive_function(self.queue.pop(0))
def callback(self, msg): try: self.process_data(msg.data) except Exception as e: self.get_logger().error(f'Processing failed: {e}')

Use create_subscription() to create subscribers Callbacks execute automatically when messages arrive Keep callbacks short and non-blocking Message types must match between publisher and subscriber Store the subscription reference to prevent garbage collection Subscribers can also publish (data processing pipelines) QoS settings must be compatible with publishers

You can send and receive data. Next, learn advanced patterns with timers and callbacks. Continue to: 2.4 Timers & Callbacks Related topics: 1.2 Topics 2.2 Publishers Chapter 2 Overview Try it yourself: Create a subscriber that receives strings and converts them to uppercase Create a subscriber that counts how many messages it receives Create a node that subscribes to one topic and publishes to another Test with ros2 topic pub command
Estimated Reading Time: 9 minutes Prerequisites: 2.1-2.3 (all previous Chapter 2 subtopics) Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Timers enable periodic execution. Callbacks handle events. Together, they make your robot responsive and efficient. This subtopic shows you advanced callback patterns. Multiple timers. Concurrent execution. Performance considerations.

Use create_timer() for periodic execution: self.timer = self.create_timer(period_seconds, callback_function) Parameters: period_seconds: How often to call (e.g., 1.0 = every second) callback_function: Function to execute

timer_node.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node class TimerNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('timer_node') # Create timer - calls every 1 second self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback) self.counter = 0 def timer_callback(self): self.counter += 1 self.get_logger().info(f'Timer tick: {self.counter}') def main(): rclpy.init() node = TimerNode() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() This prints a message every second.

You can have multiple timers with different rates: multi_timer_node.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node class MultiTimerNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('multi_timer_node') # Fast timer - 10 Hz (every 0.1 seconds) self.fast_timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.fast_callback) # Slow timer - 0.5 Hz (every 2 seconds) self.slow_timer = self.create_timer(2.0, self.slow_callback) def fast_callback(self): self.get_logger().info('Fast callback') def slow_callback(self): self.get_logger().info('Slow callback') def main(): rclpy.init() node = MultiTimerNode() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() Output: [INFO] [multi_timer_node]: Fast callback [INFO] [multi_timer_node]: Fast callback ... [INFO] [multi_timer_node]: Slow callback [INFO] [multi_timer_node]: Fast callback ... Both timers run independently.

Real nodes use all three: complete_node.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import Float32 class CompleteNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('complete_node') # Subscriber self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Float32, '/sensors/temperature', self.sensor_callback, 10 ) # Publisher self.publisher = self.create_publisher( Float32, '/processed/temperature', 10 ) # Timer - processes every 0.5 seconds self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.timer_callback) self.latest_temp = None self.temp_sum = 0.0 self.temp_count = 0 def sensor_callback(self, msg): # Store latest reading self.latest_temp = msg.data # Accumulate for averaging self.temp_sum += msg.data self.temp_count += 1 self.get_logger().debug(f'Received: {msg.data:.2f}°C') def timer_callback(self): # Process accumulated data if self.temp_count > 0: average = self.temp_sum / self.temp_count # Publish average msg = Float32() msg.data = average self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info( f'Published average: {average:.2f}°C ' f'(from {self.temp_count} samples)' ) # Reset accumulators self.temp_sum = 0.0 self.temp_count = 0 def main(): rclpy.init() node = CompleteNode() try: rclpy.spin(node) except KeyboardInterrupt: pass finally: node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()

Type: Scenario Context: Temperature sensors are noisy. You receive readings at 10 Hz. You want to publish averaged values at 2 Hz. Explanation: The subscriber receives every sensor reading. It stores them. The timer runs at 2 Hz. It calculates the average of accumulated readings. It publishes the average. Then it resets. This smooths noisy data. The timer controls the output rate independently of the input rate. Takeaway: Timers enable rate conversion and batch processing.
All callbacks (timers, subscriptions) share one thread by default. Execution rules: Callbacks execute one at a time Order is not guaranteed Long callbacks block others

Type: Problem/Solution Context: You have a fast timer (100 Hz) and a slow callback (takes 1 second). Explanation: Problem: def slow_callback(self, msg): time.sleep(1.0) # Blocks for 1 second! self.process(msg.data) def fast_callback(self): # Can't run while slow_callback blocks self.quick_task() The fast timer misses 100 ticks while the slow callback runs. Solution: Don't block in callbacks. Use timers for slow tasks: def slow_callback(self, msg): self.pending_data = msg.data # Store quickly # Don't process here def process_timer_callback(self): if self.pending_data: self.process(self.pending_data) # Process in timer self.pending_data = None Takeaway: Keep all callbacks fast. Use separate timers for slow operations.

You can stop a timer: class CancelableTimer(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('cancelable_timer') self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback) self.count = 0 def timer_callback(self): self.count += 1 self.get_logger().info(f'Tick: {self.count}') # Cancel after 5 ticks if self.count >= 5: self.timer.cancel() self.get_logger().info('Timer canceled') The timer stops after 5 executions.

Create a timer that runs once: class OneShotTimer(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('oneshot_timer') # Run once after 3 seconds self.timer = self.create_timer(3.0, self.delayed_callback) def delayed_callback(self): self.get_logger().info('Delayed action executed') # Cancel immediately after first execution self.timer.cancel() This executes once, 3 seconds after node start.

By default, callbacks run sequentially. For parallel execution, use callback groups: from rclpy.callback_groups import MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup, ReentrantCallbackGroup from rclpy.executors import MultiThreadedExecutor class ParallelNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('parallel_node') # Create callback group self.callback_group = MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup() # Timer with callback group self.timer = self.create_timer( 1.0, self.slow_callback, callback_group=self.callback_group ) def slow_callback(self): # Can run in parallel with other callbacks time.sleep(5.0) self.get_logger().info('Slow task done') def main(): rclpy.init() node = ParallelNode() # Use multi-threaded executor executor = MultiThreadedExecutor() executor.add_node(node) try: executor.spin() except KeyboardInterrupt: pass finally: executor.shutdown() node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() Use cases: When you have genuinely independent, slow tasks. Caution: Adds complexity. Only use when necessary.

Publish a heartbeat to show your node is alive: class HeartbeatNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('heartbeat_node') self.publisher = self.create_publisher( String, '/heartbeat', 10 ) # Heartbeat every 1 second self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.heartbeat_callback) def heartbeat_callback(self): msg = String() msg.data = f'Node {self.get_name()} alive' self.publisher.publish(msg) Other nodes can monitor the heartbeat to detect failures.

Monitor if timers run on time: class TimerMonitor(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('timer_monitor') self.timer = self.create_timer(0.01, self.fast_callback) # 100 Hz self.last_time = self.get_clock().now() def fast_callback(self): current_time = self.get_clock().now() elapsed = (current_time - self.last_time).nanoseconds / 1e9 if elapsed > 0.015: # More than 15ms (should be 10ms) self.get_logger().warn(f'Timer late: {elapsed:.3f}s') self.last_time = current_time This detects if your callbacks are too slow.

# Wrong - timer gets garbage collected def __init__(self): self.create_timer(1.0, self.callback) # Lost! Always store it: # Correct def __init__(self): self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.callback)
# Bad - creates new timer every callback def callback(self): self.create_timer(1.0, self.another_callback) # Don't! Create timers in __init__ only.
# Unrealistic expectation self.timer = self.create_timer(0.001, self.callback) # 1000 Hz # May not achieve exact 1000 Hz due to system load Timers are best-effort. System load affects precision.
# Good - reasonable rates sensor_timer = self.create_timer(0.01, self.sensor_callback) # 100 Hz status_timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.status_callback) # 1 Hz
# Good - quick operations def timer_callback(self): self.counter += 1 self.publish_data() # Fast
def __init__(self): super().__init__('my_node') self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.callback) self.get_logger().info('Timer created: 1 Hz')

Timers enable periodic execution with create_timer() Multiple timers can run at different rates Callbacks execute sequentially by default (one at a time) Keep callbacks short to avoid blocking other operations Store timer references to prevent garbage collection Timers can be canceled with timer.cancel() Use callback groups for parallel execution (advanced)

You've completed Chapter 2! You can create nodes, publishers, subscribers, and timers in Python. Next, learn how to organize your code into ROS 2 packages. documents.s: Chapter 3: Robot Description with URDF & Xacro

documents.t: You know how to make ROS 2 programs communicate. Now learn how to describe robot structure. URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) is XML for describing robots. Xacro makes URDF easier by adding macros and variables. This chapter teaches you to define humanoid robot models.

By the end of this chapter, you will: Understand URDF structure and syntax Define robot links and joints Use Xacro macros for reusable components Create collision and visual geometries Add inertial properties for physics Visualize robots in RViz Follow best practices for robot modeling

Learn the fundamentals of URDF, including links, joints, and the kinematic tree structure. Key Concepts: URDF syntax, link elements, joint types, parent-child relationships, coordinate frames Estimated Time: 12 minutes
Define how robots look and interact physically with their environment. Key Concepts: Visual tags, collision geometry, mesh files, primitive shapes, STL/DAE formats Estimated Time: 10 minutes
Use Xacro to create reusable, parameterized robot descriptions. Key Concepts: Xacro syntax, properties, macros, parameters, code reuse, robot variants Estimated Time: 13 minutes
Add physics properties for realistic simulation behavior. Key Concepts: Mass, inertia tensors, center of mass, physics simulation, stability Estimated Time: 10 minutes

Before starting this chapter: Complete Chapter 1 (Core Communication Patterns) Complete Chapter 2 (Python Development) Have ROS 2 Humble installed Have RViz installed (sudo apt install ros-humble-rviz2) Basic XML knowledge helpful (but not required)

Throughout this chapter, you'll create: A simple 2-link robot arm in URDF Visual and collision geometries for robot parts Xacro macros for a humanoid robot leg Complete URDF with inertial properties Visualizations in RViz

URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) is XML that describes robot structure. It defines links (rigid parts) and joints (connections between parts). Think of URDF as a blueprint. Links are like bones. Joints are like where bones connect. Together, they form a kinematic tree.

URDF is an XML format with specific tags: <robot>: Root element containing everything <link>: Rigid body part (chassis, arm, wheel) <joint>: Connection between two links <visual>: How link looks <collision>: Physical boundaries for collisions <inertial>: Mass and inertia properties

<?xml version="1.0"?> <robot name="my_robot"> <link name="base_link"> <!-- Link properties here --> </link> <joint name="joint1" type="revolute"> <!-- Joint properties here --> </joint> <link name="child_link"> <!-- Another link --> </link> </robot>
A link represents a rigid body. It has: Name: Unique identifier Visual: How it appears Collision: Boundaries for physics Inertial: Mass properties

simple_link.urdf <link name="base_link"> <visual> <geometry> <box size="0.6 0.4 0.2"/> </geometry> <material name="blue"> <color rgba="0 0 0.8 1"/> </material> </visual> </link> This creates a blue box (60cm × 40cm × 20cm).

<link name="arm_link"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.4"/> </geometry> <material name="gray"> <color rgba="0.5 0.5 0.5 1"/> </material> </visual> </link> origin: Position and rotation of geometry relative to link frame xyz: Translation (x, y, z) in meters rpy: Rotation (roll, pitch, yaw) in radians
Joints connect two links. They define: Parent link: Fixed reference Child link: Moves relative to parent Type: How child moves Limits: Movement constraints

ROS 2 supports 6 joint types: Type Description Example Use fixed No movement Sensor mount revolute Rotation with limits Elbow, knee continuous Unlimited rotation Wheel prismatic Linear motion Elevator, telescope floating 6 DOF (position + orientation) Floating base planar Movement in plane Omni wheels

revolute_joint.urdf <joint name="shoulder_joint" type="revolute"> <parent link="torso"/> <child link="upper_arm"/> <origin xyz="0 0.2 0.4" rpy="0 0 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> <limit lower="-1.57" upper="1.57" effort="100" velocity="1.0"/> </joint> Explanation: parent: Torso is fixed reference child: Upper arm moves origin: Joint location (20cm to side, 40cm up from torso origin) axis: Rotates around Y-axis (0 1 0) limit: lower/upper: ±90° (±1.57 radians) effort: Maximum torque (100 Nm) velocity: Maximum speed (1.0 rad/s)

<joint name="camera_joint" type="fixed"> <parent link="head"/> <child link="camera"/> <origin xyz="0.1 0 0.05" rpy="0 0 0"/> </joint> Fixed joints don't move. Use them for sensors or static attachments.

<joint name="wheel_joint" type="continuous"> <parent link="chassis"/> <child link="wheel"/> <origin xyz="0 0.3 -0.1" rpy="0 0 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> </joint> Continuous joints have no limits. Perfect for wheels.
URDF creates a tree structure: One root link (usually base_link) Joints define parent-child relationships Each link has exactly one parent joint (except root) Links can have multiple child joints

simple_arm.urdf <?xml version="1.0"?> <robot name="simple_arm"> <!-- Base (root link) --> <link name="base_link"> <visual> <geometry> <box size="0.2 0.2 0.1"/> </geometry> <material name="gray"> <color rgba="0.5 0.5 0.5 1"/> </material> </visual> </link> <!-- Shoulder joint connects base to upper arm --> <joint name="shoulder" type="revolute"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="upper_arm"/> <origin xyz="0 0 0.05" rpy="0 0 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> <limit lower="-1.57" upper="1.57" effort="50" velocity="1.0"/> </joint> <!-- Upper arm link --> <link name="upper_arm"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.03" length="0.3"/> </geometry> <material name="blue"> <color rgba="0 0 0.8 1"/> </material> </visual> </link> <!-- Elbow joint connects upper to lower arm --> <joint name="elbow" type="revolute"> <parent link="upper_arm"/> <child link="lower_arm"/> <origin xyz="0 0 0.3" rpy="0 0 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> <limit lower="0" upper="2.36" effort="30" velocity="1.0"/> </joint> <!-- Lower arm link --> <link name="lower_arm"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 0.12" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.025" length="0.24"/> </geometry> <material name="green"> <color rgba="0 0.8 0 1"/> </material> </visual> </link> </robot> Tree structure: base_link (root) └─ shoulder joint └─ upper_arm └─ elbow joint └─ lower_arm
Each link has its own coordinate frame. Joint origins define transformations between frames.
ROS 2 uses right-handed coordinate system: X: Forward (red) Y: Left (green) Z: Up (blue)
base_link (0, 0, 0) → shoulder joint @ (0, 0, 0.05) → upper_arm (0, 0, 0.05) → elbow joint @ (0, 0, 0.3) → lower_arm (0, 0, 0.35) Each joint adds a transformation.

ros2 launch urdf_tutorial display.launch.py model:=simple_arm.urdf This opens RViz with: Robot model displayed Joint state sliders TF frames visualization You can move the sliders to see joints articulate!

<!-- Wrong - no root link --> <robot name="bad_robot"> <joint name="joint1" type="revolute"> <parent link="nonexistent"/> <child link="link1"/> </joint> </robot> Every robot needs a root link that isn't a child of any joint.

<!-- Wrong - circular parent-child --> <joint name="j1" type="fixed"> <parent link="link_a"/> <child link="link_b"/> </joint> <joint name="j2" type="fixed"> <parent link="link_b"/> <child link="link_a"/> <!-- Circular! --> </joint> The kinematic tree must be acyclic (no loops).

<!-- Wrong - normalized axis required --> <joint name="shoulder" type="revolute"> <axis xyz="1 1 1"/> <!-- Should be normalized --> </joint> <!-- Correct --> <joint name="shoulder" type="revolute"> <axis xyz="0.577 0.577 0.577"/> <!-- Normalized --> </joint> Axis vectors should be unit length (magnitude = 1).

<!-- Wrong - child should be the moving part --> <joint name="shoulder" type="revolute"> <parent link="upper_arm"/> <!-- Moving part --> <child link="base_link"/> <!-- Fixed part --> </joint> <!-- Correct --> <joint name="shoulder" type="revolute"> <parent link="base_link"/> <!-- Fixed --> <child link="upper_arm"/> <!-- Moving --> </joint> Parent should be the fixed reference, child moves.
<!-- Good --> <link name="left_knee"/> <joint name="left_knee_pitch"/> <!-- Bad --> <link name="l1"/> <joint name="j5"/>
Links: [prefix_]part_name (e.g., left_thigh, base_link) Joints: [prefix_]part_joint[_type] (e.g., shoulder_pitch, wheel_joint)
<!-- Good - realistic limits --> <limit lower="-1.57" upper="1.57" effort="100" velocity="1.0"/> <!-- Bad - unrealistic --> <limit lower="-100" upper="100" effort="9999" velocity="1000"/>

Place link origins at joint centers for easier calculations: <link name="thigh"> <visual> <!-- Geometry centered at joint --> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.4"/> </geometry> </visual> </link>

URDF is XML for describing robot structure Links are rigid body parts with visual/collision/inertial properties Joints connect links with parent-child relationships Joint types: fixed, revolute, continuous, prismatic, floating, planar URDF forms a kinematic tree (no loops) Each link has its own coordinate frame Use check_urdf to validate syntax Visualize in RViz with display.launch.py

Robots need two types of geometry: Visual: How the robot looks (rendering) Collision: Physical boundaries (physics simulation) These can be different. Visual geometry is detailed. Collision geometry is simplified for performance.
Visual geometry defines appearance. It's used for: RViz visualization Simulation rendering User interfaces

URDF supports basic shapes: Box​ <visual> <geometry> <box size="length width height"/> </geometry> <material name="red"> <color rgba="1 0 0 1"/> </material> </visual> Example - Chassis: <link name="chassis"> <visual> <geometry> <box size="0.6 0.4 0.2"/> </geometry> <material name="gray"> <color rgba="0.7 0.7 0.7 1"/> </material> </visual> </link> Cylinder​ <visual> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.3"/> </geometry> </visual> Example - Wheel: <link name="wheel"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="1.57 0 0"/> <!-- Rotate 90° to align --> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.1" length="0.05"/> </geometry> <material name="black"> <color rgba="0.1 0.1 0.1 1"/> </material> </visual> </link> tip Cylinders are aligned with Z-axis by default. Rotate to align with other axes. Sphere​ <visual> <geometry> <sphere radius="0.1"/> </geometry> </visual> Example - Joint Sphere: <link name="shoulder_ball"> <visual> <geometry> <sphere radius="0.06"/> </geometry> <material name="white"> <color rgba="0.9 0.9 0.9 1"/> </material> </visual> </link>

For complex shapes, use 3D mesh files: <visual> <geometry> <mesh filename="package://my_robot_description/meshes/head.dae" scale="1 1 1"/> </geometry> </visual> Supported formats: STL: Simple, no color (ASCII or binary) DAE (Collada): Supports colors, textures, animations OBJ: Wavefront format with materials Example - Robot Head: <link name="head"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 0.05" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <mesh filename="package://humanoid_description/meshes/head.dae"/> </geometry> </visual> </link> Package Path Syntax​ package://<package_name>/relative/path/to/file Examples: package://my_robot/meshes/arm.stl package://humanoid_description/meshes/torso.dae warning Mesh paths use package:// URIs, not absolute file paths. This ensures portability across systems. Mesh Scaling​ <mesh filename="package://robot/meshes/part.dae" scale="0.001 0.001 0.001"/> Common scales: 1 1 1: Default (meters if exported in meters) 0.001 0.001 0.001: Millimeters to meters conversion 2 2 2: Double size

Define materials inline or globally: Inline Material​ <visual> <geometry> <box size="0.5 0.3 0.2"/> </geometry> <material name="blue"> <color rgba="0 0 0.8 1"/> </material> </visual> Global Material (Reusable)​ <robot name="my_robot"> <!-- Define material once --> <material name="orange"> <color rgba="1.0 0.5 0.0 1.0"/> </material> <!-- Use multiple times --> <link name="link1"> <visual> <geometry><box size="0.1 0.1 0.1"/></geometry> <material name="orange"/> </visual> </link> <link name="link2"> <visual> <geometry><box size="0.2 0.1 0.1"/></geometry> <material name="orange"/> </visual> </link> </robot> RGBA Format​ <color rgba="red green blue alpha"/> red, green, blue: 0.0 to 1.0 alpha: 0.0 (transparent) to 1.0 (opaque) Examples: <color rgba="1 0 0 1"/> <!-- Red --> <color rgba="0 1 0 1"/> <!-- Green --> <color rgba="0 0 1 1"/> <!-- Blue --> <color rgba="1 1 1 1"/> <!-- White --> <color rgba="0 0 0 1"/> <!-- Black --> <color rgba="0.5 0.5 0.5 1"/> <!-- Gray --> <color rgba="1 0.5 0 0.5"/> <!-- Orange, 50% transparent -->
Collision geometry defines physical boundaries for: Physics simulation Collision detection Contact forces
Performance: Simplified shapes compute faster Accuracy: Complex visual meshes slow down physics
<collision> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <box size="0.5 0.3 0.2"/> </geometry> </collision> Same geometry types as visual: box, cylinder, sphere, mesh.

<link name="robot_arm"> <!-- Detailed visual --> <visual> <geometry> <mesh filename="package://robot/meshes/arm_detailed.dae"/> </geometry> <material name="silver"> <color rgba="0.8 0.8 0.9 1"/> </material> </visual> <!-- Simplified collision --> <collision> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.4"/> </geometry> </collision> </link> Visual uses detailed mesh. Collision uses simple cylinder.

1. Use Primitive Shapes When Possible​ <!-- Good - fast physics --> <collision> <geometry> <box size="0.6 0.4 0.2"/> </geometry> </collision> <!-- Avoid - slow physics --> <collision> <geometry> <mesh filename="package://robot/meshes/chassis_complex.stl"/> </geometry> </collision> 2. Approximate Complex Shapes​ Break complex shapes into multiple simple collision elements: <link name="humanoid_torso"> <!-- Visual: detailed mesh --> <visual> <geometry> <mesh filename="package://humanoid/meshes/torso.dae"/> </geometry> </visual> <!-- Collision: approximation with 3 boxes --> <collision name="torso_upper"> <origin xyz="0 0 0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <box size="0.3 0.4 0.2"/> </geometry> </collision> <collision name="torso_middle"> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <box size="0.3 0.4 0.15"/> </geometry> </collision> <collision name="torso_lower"> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <box size="0.28 0.35 0.1"/> </geometry> </collision> </link> 3. Match Approximate Bounds​ Collision should roughly match visual bounds: <link name="leg_segment"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.045" length="0.4"/> </geometry> </visual> <!-- Collision slightly larger for safety margin --> <collision> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.4"/> </geometry> </collision> </link>

complete_link.urdf <link name="forearm"> <!-- Visual: detailed appearance --> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <mesh filename="package://humanoid/meshes/forearm.dae" scale="1 1 1"/> </geometry> <material name="skin_tone"> <color rgba="0.95 0.8 0.7 1"/> </material> </visual> <!-- Collision: simplified for physics --> <collision> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.04" length="0.3"/> </geometry> </collision> <!-- Inertial properties (covered in 3.4) --> <inertial> <mass value="0.8"/> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <inertia ixx="0.002" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.002" iyz="0" izz="0.0003"/> </inertial> </link>

URDF files get long and repetitive. Humanoid robots have symmetric parts (left/right legs, arms). Writing everything twice causes errors. Xacro (XML Macros) solves this. It adds: Properties: Variables for reusable values Macros: Templates for repeated structures Math: Calculate derived values Includes: Split files for organization Xacro files use .xacro extension. They compile to URDF.
Xacro is a preprocessing language for URDF. It generates URDF from templates. Workflow: robot.urdf.xacro → [xacro processor] → robot.urdf → ROS 2

simple.urdf.xacro <?xml version="1.0"?> <robot xmlns:xacro="http://www.ros.org/wiki/xacro" name="my_robot"> <xacro:property name="width" value="0.3"/> <link name="base_link"> <visual> <geometry> <box size="${width} ${width} 0.1"/> </geometry> </visual> </link> </robot> Key elements: xmlns:xacro: Declares Xacro namespace <xacro:property>: Define variable ${variable}: Use variable value
xacro robot.urdf.xacro > robot.urdf Or directly in launch files (recommended): robot_description = Command(['xacro ', robot_file])
<xacro:property name="pi" value="3.14159"/> <xacro:property name="wheel_radius" value="0.1"/> <xacro:property name="base_width" value="0.5"/> <xacro:property name="leg_length" value="0.4"/>

<link name="wheel"> <visual> <geometry> <cylinder radius="${wheel_radius}" length="0.05"/> </geometry> </visual> </link> <joint name="wheel_joint" type="continuous"> <origin xyz="0 ${base_width/2} -${wheel_radius}" rpy="0 0 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> </joint> Math in properties: <!-- Division --> <origin xyz="0 ${base_width/2} 0"/> <!-- Multiplication --> <origin xyz="0 0 ${leg_length*2}"/> <!-- Addition/Subtraction --> <origin xyz="0 ${base_width/2 + 0.1} 0"/>

Properties can be: Global: Defined at robot level Local: Defined within macros <!-- Global property --> <xacro:property name="arm_length" value="0.3"/> <xacro:macro name="arm" params="prefix"> <!-- Local property (only within macro) --> <xacro:property name="segment_length" value="${arm_length/2}"/> <link name="${prefix}_upper_arm"> <visual> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.04" length="${segment_length}"/> </geometry> </visual> </link> </xacro:macro>
Macros are parameterized templates for repeated structures.

<xacro:macro name="wheel" params="prefix reflect"> <link name="${prefix}_wheel"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="1.57 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.1" length="0.05"/> </geometry> <material name="black"> <color rgba="0.1 0.1 0.1 1"/> </material> </visual> <collision> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="1.57 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.1" length="0.05"/> </geometry> </collision> </link> <joint name="${prefix}_wheel_joint" type="continuous"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="${prefix}_wheel"/> <origin xyz="0 ${reflect*0.3} -0.1" rpy="0 0 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> </joint> </xacro:macro> Macro elements: name: Macro identifier params: Space-separated parameter list ${param}: Parameter substitution

<!-- Create left wheel (reflect=1) --> <xacro:wheel prefix="left" reflect="1"/> <!-- Create right wheel (reflect=-1) --> <xacro:wheel prefix="right" reflect="-1"/> This generates 2 wheels, mirrored across Y-axis.

<xacro:macro name="leg" params="prefix reflect:=1 mass:=2.0"> <link name="${prefix}_thigh"> <inertial> <mass value="${mass}"/> ... </inertial> ... </link> <joint name="${prefix}_hip" type="revolute"> <origin xyz="0 ${reflect*0.15} 0" rpy="0 0 0"/> ... </joint> </xacro:macro> Default syntax: param:=default_value Usage: <!-- Use defaults --> <xacro:leg prefix="left"/> <!-- Override mass --> <xacro:leg prefix="right" mass="2.5"/> <!-- Override both --> <xacro:leg prefix="left" reflect="-1" mass="1.8"/>

Xacro supports conditional logic: <xacro:macro name="sensor" params="type"> <link name="sensor_link"> <visual> <geometry> <xacro:if value="${type == 'camera'}"> <box size="0.05 0.1 0.03"/> </xacro:if> <xacro:unless value="${type == 'camera'}"> <cylinder radius="0.03" length="0.08"/> </xacro:unless> </geometry> </visual> </link> </xacro:macro> <!-- Create camera sensor --> <xacro:sensor type="camera"/> <!-- Create LIDAR sensor --> <xacro:sensor type="lidar"/>
Split large robots into multiple files:

Visual and collision geometry define appearance and boundaries. Inertial properties define how robots behave in physics simulation. Every link needs: Mass: How heavy it is Center of Mass: Balance point Inertia Tensor: Resistance to rotation Without proper inertial properties, robots behave unrealistically in Gazebo or Isaac Sim.

Without inertia: Robot parts float, spin wildly, ignore gravity With inertia: Realistic movement, stable simulation, accurate dynamics Physics engines (Gazebo, Isaac Sim) use inertial properties to calculate: Gravity effects Collision responses Joint torques Balance and stability

<link name="my_link"> <inertial> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="0 0 0"/> <mass value="1.0"/> <inertia ixx="0.01" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.01" iyz="0" izz="0.01"/> </inertial> <!-- Visual and collision also defined --> </link> Components: <origin>: Center of mass location relative to link frame <mass>: Total mass in kilograms <inertia>: 3×3 inertia tensor (moment of inertia)
Mass is straightforward: total weight in kg.
Robot Part Typical Mass (kg) Humanoid torso 5-15 Humanoid thigh 2-4 Humanoid shin 1-2 Humanoid foot 0.3-0.8 Humanoid head 1-3 Arm upper 1-2 Arm lower 0.5-1 Hand 0.2-0.5
The center of mass is the balance point. For symmetric shapes, it's usually at the geometric center.

<!-- Cylinder centered at origin --> <link name="leg_segment"> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.4"/> </geometry> </visual> <inertial> <!-- COM at center of cylinder --> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <mass value="1.5"/> ... </inertial> </link> COM should match the visual geometry center.

For complex meshes or asymmetric parts, COM may not be at the origin. <link name="foot"> <visual> <origin xyz="0.05 0 0" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <box size="0.2 0.1 0.05"/> </geometry> </visual> <inertial> <!-- COM slightly forward due to foot shape --> <origin xyz="0.06 0 -0.01" rpy="0 0 0"/> <mass value="0.5"/> ... </inertial> </link>

The inertia tensor describes resistance to rotation. It's a 3×3 symmetric matrix: ⎡ Ixx Ixy Ixz ⎤ ⎢ Ixy Iyy Iyz ⎥ ⎣ Ixz Iyz Izz ⎦ In URDF: <inertia ixx="value" ixy="value" ixz="value" iyy="value" iyz="value" izz="value"/>
Ixx: Resistance to rotation around X-axis Iyy: Resistance to rotation around Y-axis Izz: Resistance to rotation around Z-axis Larger values = harder to rotate
Ixy, Ixz, Iyz: Coupling between axes For symmetric shapes aligned with axes, these are usually 0.

For simple shapes, use physics formulas: Solid Cylinder (around center)​ Ixx = Iyy = (1/12) * m * (3*r² + h²) Izz = (1/2) * m * r² Where: m = mass r = radius h = height (length) Example: Leg segment (cylinder) Mass: 1.5 kg Radius: 0.05 m Length: 0.4 m m = 1.5 r = 0.05 h = 0.4 Ixx = Iyy = (1/12) * m * (3*r**2 + h**2) = (1/12) * 1.5 * (3*0.0025 + 0.16) = 0.0209 kg⋅m² Izz = (1/2) * m * r**2 = (1/2) * 1.5 * 0.0025 = 0.0019 kg⋅m² <inertial> <mass value="1.5"/> <inertia ixx="0.0209" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.0209" iyz="0" izz="0.0019"/> </inertial> Solid Box (around center)​ Ixx = (1/12) * m * (h² + d²) Iyy = (1/12) * m * (w² + d²) Izz = (1/12) * m * (w² + h²) Where: w = width (x) h = height (y) d = depth (z) Example: Torso (box) Mass: 10 kg Size: 0.3 × 0.5 × 0.6 m m = 10 w = 0.3 h = 0.5 d = 0.6 Ixx = (1/12) * m * (h**2 + d**2) = (1/12) * 10 * (0.25 + 0.36) = 0.508 kg⋅m² Iyy = (1/12) * m * (w**2 + d**2) = (1/12) * 10 * (0.09 + 0.36) = 0.375 kg⋅m² Izz = (1/12) * m * (w**2 + h**2) = (1/12) * 10 * (0.09 + 0.25) = 0.283 kg⋅m² <inertial> <mass value="10"/> <inertia ixx="0.508" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.375" iyz="0" izz="0.283"/> </inertial> Solid Sphere​ Ixx = Iyy = Izz = (2/5) * m * r² Example: Head (sphere) Mass: 2 kg Radius: 0.1 m m = 2 r = 0.1 I = (2/5) * m * r**2 = (2/5) * 2 * 0.01 = 0.008 kg⋅m² <inertial> <mass value="2"/> <inertia ixx="0.008" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.008" iyz="0" izz="0.008"/> </inertial>

Most CAD tools calculate inertial properties automatically: SolidWorks: Tools → Mass Properties Fusion 360: Inspect → Physical Properties FreeCAD: View → Measure → Mass Properties Export values and use in URDF.
For complex meshes: Import mesh in MeshLab Filters → Quality Measure → Compute Geometric Measures Use mass and inertia values Or use SolidWorks URDF exporter plugin.

Create reusable inertia calculators: inertial_macros.xacro <robot xmlns:xacro="http://www.ros.org/wiki/xacro"> <!-- Box inertia --> <xacro:macro name="box_inertial" params="mass x y z"> <inertial> <mass value="${mass}"/> <inertia ixx="${mass * (y*y + z*z) / 12.0}" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="${mass * (x*x + z*z) / 12.0}" iyz="0" izz="${mass * (x*x + y*y) / 12.0}"/> </inertial> </xacro:macro> <!-- Cylinder inertia (aligned with Z-axis) --> <xacro:macro name="cylinder_inertial" params="mass r h"> <inertial> <mass value="${mass}"/> <inertia ixx="${mass * (3*r*r + h*h) / 12.0}" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="${mass * (3*r*r + h*h) / 12.0}" iyz="0" izz="${mass * r*r / 2.0}"/> </inertial> </xacro:macro> <!-- Sphere inertia --> <xacro:macro name="sphere_inertial" params="mass r"> <inertial> <mass value="${mass}"/> <inertia ixx="${2.0 * mass * r*r / 5.0}" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="${2.0 * mass * r*r / 5.0}" iyz="0" izz="${2.0 * mass * r*r / 5.0}"/> </inertial> </xacro:macro> </robot> Usage: <xacro:include filename="inertial_macros.xacro"/> <link name="torso"> <visual> <geometry> <box size="0.3 0.5 0.6"/> </geometry> </visual> <!-- Use macro --> <xacro:box_inertial mass="10" x="0.3" y="0.5" z="0.6"/> </link> <link name="thigh"> <visual> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.4"/> </geometry> </visual> <!-- Use macro --> <xacro:cylinder_inertial mass="2.5" r="0.05" h="0.4"/> </link>

<link name="upper_arm"> <!-- Visual --> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.04" length="0.3"/> </geometry> <material name="gray"> <color rgba="0.7 0.7 0.7 1"/> </material> </visual> <!-- Collision --> <collision> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.04" length="0.3"/> </geometry> </collision> <!-- Inertial --> <inertial> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/> <mass value="1.2"/> <inertia ixx="0.0091" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.0091" iyz="0" izz="0.00096"/> </inertial> </link> All three (visual, collision, inertial) have the same origin (cylinder center).
Inertia tensor must be positive definite. Simple check: Ixx > 0 Iyy > 0 Izz > 0 Ixx + Iyy >= Izz Iyy + Izz >= Ixx Izz + Ixx >= Iyy
Spawn robot in Gazebo Check for warnings: Warning: Inertia matrix is not positive definite If stable, inertia is reasonable

Drop robot from height in simulation. It should: Fall realistically Not rotate wildly Collide and stop If behavior is wrong, check: Mass too small/large COM offset incorrectly Inertia values unrealistic

<!-- Wrong - causes simulation errors --> <inertial> <mass value="1.0"/> <inertia ixx="0" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0" iyz="0" izz="0"/> </inertial> Even small links need non-zero inertia. Use small values: <inertia ixx="0.001" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.001" iyz="0" izz="0.001"/>
<!-- Wrong - unrealistic --> <mass value="1000"/> <!-- 1 ton for a robot arm? --> Use realistic values based on real robot specifications.

<!-- Wrong - COM doesn't match geometry --> <visual> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <geometry> <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.4"/> </geometry> </visual> <inertial> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="0 0 0"/> <!-- Wrong origin --> <mass value="1.5"/> ... </inertial> COM should be at cylinder center: <inertial> <origin xyz="0 0 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <!-- Correct --> ... </inertial>

<!-- Wrong - sensor link with no inertia --> <link name="camera"> <visual>...</visual> <!-- Missing inertial! --> </link> Even small sensor links need minimal inertia: <link name="camera"> <visual>...</visual> <inertial> <mass value="0.1"/> <inertia ixx="0.0001" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.0001" iyz="0" izz="0.0001"/> </inertial> </link>
Research similar robots or use CAD mass properties.
Don't recalculate inertia manually. Use Xacro macros.
For symmetric shapes, COM should be at visual geometry center.
Always validate robot behavior in Gazebo before deployment.

<!-- Thigh: solid aluminum cylinder, 2.5 kg Dimensions: r=0.05m, h=0.4m Inertia calculated using standard formula --> <link name="thigh"> <xacro:cylinder_inertial mass="2.5" r="0.05" h="0.4"/> ... </link>

import numpy as np def box_inertia(mass, x, y, z): return { 'ixx': mass * (y**2 + z**2) / 12.0, 'iyy': mass * (x**2 + z**2) / 12.0, 'izz': mass * (x**2 + y**2) / 12.0, } def cylinder_inertia(mass, r, h): return { 'ixx': mass * (3*r**2 + h**2) / 12.0, 'iyy': mass * (3*r**2 + h**2) / 12.0, 'izz': mass * r**2 / 2.0, } # Example usage torso = box_inertia(10, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6) print(f"Torso inertia: {torso}")

Inertial properties enable realistic physics simulation Every link needs: mass, center of mass, inertia tensor Mass: Total weight in kg COM: Balance point (often at geometry center) Inertia: 3×3 tensor (resistance to rotation) Diagonal terms (Ixx, Iyy, Izz) are main moments Off-diagonal terms (Ixy, Ixz, Iyz) are usually 0 for symmetric shapes Use standard formulas for simple shapes Use CAD software for complex meshes Create Xacro macros for reusable inertia calculations Validate in Gazebo before deployment

Welcome to Chapter 4! Now that you've learned about ROS 2 core concepts, Python programming with rclpy, and robot modeling with URDF/Xacro, it's time to understand how to organize and build real ROS 2 projects.

In this chapter, you'll learn how to structure, build, and manage ROS 2 packages—the fundamental units of organization in ROS 2. Think of packages as containers that hold your nodes, launch files, configuration files, and other resources in a structured way. Estimated Time: 35-40 minutes

Ready to build real ROS 2 projects? Let's dive into package structure and workspaces! Next: 4.1 Package Structure & Workspace →

Estimated reading time: 10 minutes Think of a ROS 2 package as a folder that contains all the code, configuration files, and resources for a specific piece of functionality. Just like you wouldn't throw all your files onto your desktop, you wouldn't throw all your ROS 2 code into one giant file. Packages help you organize and modularize your robotics projects.

A package is the fundamental unit of organization in ROS 2. It's a directory that contains: Nodes: Your executable programs Launch files: Scripts to start multiple nodes Configuration files: Parameters and settings Message/Service definitions: Custom data types Documentation: README files and guides Each package should have a single, well-defined purpose. For example: robot_sensors: Code for all sensor drivers robot_navigation: Navigation algorithms robot_description: URDF models and meshes robot_control: Motor controllers
Before diving into packages, let's understand the workspace—the top-level folder that contains your packages.

A typical ROS 2 workspace looks like this: my_robot_ws/ # Workspace root ├── src/ # Source space (your packages go here) │ ├── package1/ │ ├── package2/ │ └── package3/ ├── build/ # Build space (temporary build files) ├── install/ # Install space (compiled packages) └── log/ # Log files from builds Key Directories: src/: Where you create and edit your packages (the only directory you commit to git) build/: Contains intermediate build files (auto-generated, ignored by git) install/: Contains the final compiled packages ready to use (auto-generated) log/: Build logs for debugging (auto-generated) tip Only the src/ directory should be tracked in version control. Add build/, install/, and log/ to your .gitignore file.

Here's how to create a new workspace: # Create workspace directory mkdir -p ~/my_robot_ws/src cd ~/my_robot_ws/src # Initialize the workspace (optional but good practice) cd ~/my_robot_ws colcon build # Creates build, install, and log directories # Source the workspace source install/setup.bash

Let's explore what's inside a typical Python package: my_robot_package/ ├── package.xml # Package metadata and dependencies ├── setup.py # Python installation configuration ├── setup.cfg # Python package configuration ├── resource/ # Package resource marker │ └── my_robot_package ├── my_robot_package/ # Python module directory │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── node1.py │ └── node2.py └── test/ # Unit tests ├── test_node1.py └── test_node2.py

1. package.xml​ This XML file contains metadata about your package: <?xml version="1.0"?> <?xml-model href="http://download.ros.org/schema/package_format3.xsd" schematypens="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"?> <package format="3"> <name>my_robot_package</name> <version>0.0.1</version> <description>A sample robot package</description> <maintainer email="you@example.com">Your Name</maintainer> <license>Apache-2.0</license> <!-- Build tool dependency --> <buildtool_depend>ament_cmake</buildtool_depend> <!-- Package dependencies --> <depend>rclpy</depend> <depend>std_msgs</depend> <!-- Test dependencies --> <test_depend>ament_lint_auto</test_depend> <test_depend>ament_lint_common</test_depend> <export> <build_type>ament_python</build_type> </export> </package> Important fields: <name>: Package name (must match directory name) <version>: Semantic version (major.minor.patch) <description>: Brief explanation of what the package does <maintainer>: Who maintains this package <license>: Software license (Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD, etc.) <depend>: Package dependencies (more in section 4.2) 2. setup.py​ For Python packages, this file configures the Python installation: from setuptools import setup package_name = 'my_robot_package' setup( name=package_name, version='0.0.1', packages=[package_name], data_files=[ ('share/ament_index/resource_index/packages', ['resource/' + package_name]), ('share/' + package_name, ['package.xml']), ], install_requires=['setuptools'], zip_safe=True, maintainer='Your Name', maintainer_email='you@example.com', description='A sample robot package', license='Apache-2.0', tests_require=['pytest'], entry_points={ 'console_scripts': [ 'my_node = my_robot_package.node1:main', ], }, ) Key section: entry_points defines executable nodes: Left side: Command name you'll use (ros2 run my_robot_package my_node) Right side: Python module path and function (my_robot_package.node1:main) 3. setup.cfg​ Simple configuration file for Python packages: [develop] script_dir=$base/lib/my_robot_package [install] install_scripts=$base/lib/my_robot_package This tells Python where to install executable scripts.
ROS 2 provides a convenient tool to create packages with the correct structure:

cd ~/my_robot_ws/src ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python my_robot_package \ --dependencies rclpy std_msgs Flags explained: --build-type ament_python: Create a Python package --dependencies: List of packages this package depends on
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_cmake my_cpp_package \ --dependencies rclcpp std_msgs Difference: C++ packages use ament_cmake and have a CMakeLists.txt instead of setup.py.

After running the command, you'll see: Creating my_robot_package... going to create a new package package name: my_robot_package destination directory: /home/user/my_robot_ws/src package format: 3 version: 0.0.0 description: TODO: Package description maintainer: ['user <user@todo.todo>'] licenses: ['TODO: License declaration'] build type: ament_python dependencies: ['rclpy', 'std_msgs'] warning Don't forget to update the TODO fields in package.xml with real information!

Python Package: Rapid prototyping High-level decision making Not performance-critical Easier to debug and modify C++ Package: Real-time control loops Image/sensor processing Hardware drivers Performance-critical code Hybrid Package: Large projects with both high-level and low-level code When you need both Python and C++ in the same package

Let's add a simple publisher node to our package: # my_robot_package/publisher_node.py import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import String class PublisherNode(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('publisher_node') self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, 'chatter', 10) self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback) self.counter = 0 def timer_callback(self): msg = String() msg.data = f'Hello ROS 2: {self.counter}' self.publisher.publish(msg) self.get_logger().info(f'Publishing: "{msg.data}"') self.counter += 1 def main(args=None): rclpy.init(args=args) node = PublisherNode() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main() Now register it in setup.py: entry_points={ 'console_scripts': [ 'publisher_node = my_robot_package.publisher_node:main', ], }, Build and run: cd ~/my_robot_ws colcon build --packages-select my_robot_package source install/setup.bash ros2 run my_robot_package publisher_node

Always include a README.md in your package: # My Robot Package ## Overview Brief description of what this package does. ## Nodes - `publisher_node`: Publishes messages to the chatter topic ## Topics - `/chatter` (std_msgs/String): Chat messages ## Usage \`\`\`bash ros2 run my_robot_package publisher_node \`\`\`
# Directory name: my_package # package.xml name: my_robot_package ❌ WRONG! Solution: Directory name and <name> in package.xml must match exactly.
colcon build ros2 run my_package my_node # ❌ Package not found! Solution: Always source after building: source install/setup.bash
Using ament_python for a C++ package or vice versa. Solution: Match build type to your code language.

Create a package with both a publisher and subscriber: Create package: ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python chat_system --dependencies rclpy std_msgs Add a publisher node (sends messages) Add a subscriber node (receives messages) Register both in setup.py Build and test

Create a package with this structure: sensor_package/ ├── sensor_package/ │ ├── drivers/ │ │ ├── camera_driver.py │ │ └── lidar_driver.py │ └── processors/ │ └── data_processor.py Implement at least one working node in each subdirectory.

In this section, you learned: ROS 2 packages are the fundamental units of organization Workspaces contain packages in the src/ directory package.xml defines package metadata and dependencies setup.py configures Python package installation Use ros2 pkg create to generate package structure Python and C++ packages have different build systems Proper package organization improves maintainability

Now that you understand package structure, let's learn how to manage dependencies between packages in 4.2 Dependencies & package.xml → Navigation ← Back to Chapter 4 Overview Next: 4.2 Dependencies & package.xml →

Estimated reading time: 8 minutes Imagine building a house without ordering materials first—you'd quickly realize you need bricks, cement, and wood before you can start. Similarly, your ROS 2 packages often need other packages to function. This is where dependencies come in. In this section, you'll learn how to declare, manage, and troubleshoot dependencies in your ROS 2 packages.

Dependencies tell ROS 2: What other packages your package needs to build What other packages your package needs to run What tools are needed for testing Without proper dependency declarations, your package might: Fail to build on another computer Crash at runtime due to missing libraries Be impossible to test or deploy tip Think of dependencies as a recipe's ingredient list—anyone should be able to look at your package.xml and know exactly what's needed.
ROS 2 has several dependency types, each serving a different purpose:

Needed to compile your package: <build_depend>rclcpp</build_depend> <build_depend>std_msgs</build_depend> When to use: Your code includes headers or imports from these packages at build time. Example: If your C++ code has #include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>, you need rclcpp as a build dependency.

Needed to run your package: <exec_depend>rclpy</exec_depend> <exec_depend>sensor_msgs</exec_depend> When to use: Your package imports or uses these packages at runtime. Example: If your Python node has import rclpy, you need rclpy as an execution dependency.

Shorthand when you need a package for both building and running: <depend>rclpy</depend> <depend>std_msgs</depend> This is equivalent to: <build_depend>rclpy</build_depend> <exec_depend>rclpy</exec_depend> tip Use <depend> for most dependencies to keep your package.xml clean. Only separate into build/exec when you specifically need different dependencies for building vs running.

Needed only for testing: <test_depend>ament_lint_auto</test_depend> <test_depend>ament_lint_common</test_depend> <test_depend>pytest</test_depend> When to use: Testing frameworks and tools that aren't needed for normal operation.

Build system tools: <buildtool_depend>ament_cmake</buildtool_depend> <!-- OR --> <buildtool_depend>ament_python</buildtool_depend> When to use: Always required—specifies the build system (CMake or Python).

Here's a well-structured package.xml with various dependency types: <?xml version="1.0"?> <?xml-model href="http://download.ros.org/schema/package_format3.xsd" schematypens="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"?> <package format="3"> <name>robot_controller</name> <version>1.0.0</version> <description>Controller package for mobile robot</description> <maintainer email="roboticist@example.com">Jane Roboticist</maintainer> <license>Apache-2.0</license> <!-- Build tool --> <buildtool_depend>ament_python</buildtool_depend> <!-- Core ROS 2 dependencies (needed for build and run) --> <depend>rclpy</depend> <!-- Message/Service packages --> <depend>std_msgs</depend> <depend>geometry_msgs</depend> <depend>sensor_msgs</depend> <!-- Only needed at runtime --> <exec_depend>robot_description</exec_depend> <!-- Testing --> <test_depend>ament_lint_auto</test_depend> <test_depend>ament_lint_common</test_depend> <test_depend>pytest</test_depend> <export> <build_type>ament_python</build_type> </export> </package>
Here are packages you'll frequently depend on:

Package Purpose rclpy Python client library (always needed) std_msgs Standard message types (String, Int32, etc.) geometry_msgs Geometric messages (Pose, Twist, etc.) sensor_msgs Sensor messages (Image, LaserScan, etc.) nav_msgs Navigation messages (Odometry, Path, etc.) tf2_ros Transform library for coordinate frames

Package Purpose rclcpp C++ client library (always needed) std_msgs Standard message types geometry_msgs Geometric messages sensor_msgs Sensor messages tf2_ros Transform library cv_bridge Convert between ROS and OpenCV images
rosdep is a tool that installs system dependencies for ROS packages. It maps ROS package names to system package names.

Before building a workspace, install all dependencies: cd ~/my_robot_ws # Update rosdep database rosdep update # Install all dependencies for packages in src/ rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y Flags explained: --from-paths src: Look for packages in the src directory --ignore-src: Don't install packages that are in your workspace -r: Continue despite errors -y: Automatically say yes to installation prompts

# For a package that depends on rclpy, rosdep will: # 1. Look up the system package for rclpy # 2. Install it using your system's package manager # On Ubuntu: sudo apt install ros-humble-rclpy # On other systems: # Uses appropriate package manager (dnf, pacman, brew, etc.) tip Always run rosdep install before building a new workspace or after cloning a project. It ensures all dependencies are installed.
Not sure what dependencies you need? Here are ways to discover them:
For Python packages, look at your imports: import rclpy # Need: rclpy from std_msgs.msg import String # Need: std_msgs from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist # Need: geometry_msgs
Find information about any package: # List all packages ros2 pkg list # Get package location ros2 pkg prefix std_msgs # Get package executables ros2 pkg executables rclpy
Look at the ROS 2 package index: # Or use the command line ros2 pkg xml std_msgs
A circular dependency occurs when Package A depends on Package B, and Package B depends on Package A: Package A → depends on → Package B Package B → depends on → Package A ❌ CIRCULAR!
Circular dependencies: Prevent proper build ordering Make code harder to maintain Indicate poor architecture

Solution 1: Extract Common Code Before: package_a ←→ package_b After: package_a → common_package package_b → common_package Solution 2: Merge Packages If two packages are tightly coupled, they might belong together: package_a + package_b = unified_package Solution 3: Invert Dependency Sometimes one package should depend on the other, not both: package_a → package_b ✓ (package_a depends on package_b)

Only declare dependencies you actually use: <!-- BAD: Listing everything just in case --> <depend>rclpy</depend> <depend>std_msgs</depend> <depend>geometry_msgs</depend> <depend>sensor_msgs</depend> <depend>nav_msgs</depend> <depend>tf2_ros</depend> <!-- ... when you only use rclpy and std_msgs --> <!-- GOOD: Only what you need --> <depend>rclpy</depend> <depend>std_msgs</depend>

Don't rely on transitive dependencies: # If you use geometry_msgs... from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist # ...declare it explicitly in package.xml: <depend>geometry_msgs</depend> # Don't assume it comes through another package!

You can specify version requirements: <depend version_gte="1.0.0">my_package</depend> <!-- >= 1.0.0 --> <depend version_lte="2.0.0">my_package</depend> <!-- <= 2.0.0 --> <depend version_eq="1.5.0">my_package</depend> <!-- == 1.5.0 -->

Group related dependencies: <!-- Core ROS 2 --> <depend>rclpy</depend> <!-- Message types --> <depend>std_msgs</depend> <depend>sensor_msgs</depend> <!-- Custom packages --> <depend>robot_description</depend> <depend>robot_interfaces</depend> <!-- Testing --> <test_depend>pytest</test_depend>

Symptom: Build or runtime error: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'geometry_msgs' Solution: Add to package.xml: <depend>geometry_msgs</depend> Then install and rebuild: rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y colcon build source install/setup.bash

Symptom: ERROR: the following packages/stacks could not have their rosdep keys resolved to system dependencies: my_custom_package: Cannot locate rosdep definition for [my_custom_package] Solution: This is expected for your own packages. Use --ignore-src: rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y

Create a package that depends on multiple message types: ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python multi_msg_node Add code that uses: std_msgs/String geometry_msgs/Twist sensor_msgs/LaserScan Update package.xml with correct dependencies, then build.

Given this Python node, identify all required dependencies: import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from sensor_msgs.msg import Image from geometry_msgs.msg import Pose from cv_bridge import CvBridge import cv2 class ImageProcessor(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('image_processor') self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Image, 'camera/image', self.image_callback, 10) self.bridge = CvBridge() Answer: <depend>rclpy</depend> <depend>sensor_msgs</depend> <depend>geometry_msgs</depend> <depend>cv_bridge</depend>
You have: robot_brain depends on robot_sensors robot_sensors depends on robot_brain Redesign the architecture to eliminate the circular dependency.

Verify your dependencies are correct: # Check what packages are installed ros2 pkg list | grep my_package # Verify dependency resolution rosdep check --from-paths src --ignore-src # See dependency tree colcon graph --packages-select my_package

Now that you understand dependencies, let's learn how to build packages efficiently with colcon in 4.3 Building with colcon → Navigation ← Back: 4.1 Package Structure Next: 4.3 Building with colcon →

Estimated reading time: 9 minutes You've created packages and declared dependencies—now it's time to build them into working software. Meet colcon, ROS 2's build tool that transforms your source code into executable nodes. Think of colcon as a smart construction manager: it figures out the order to build packages (based on dependencies), compiles code, runs tests, and installs everything in the right place.

colcon (collective construction) is a command-line tool that: Builds multiple packages in the correct order Supports different build systems (Python, CMake, etc.) Handles dependencies between packages Runs tests and generates reports Works across different operating systems Unlike tools that only handle one language, colcon can build Python, C++, and mixed workspaces—all in one command.

The most common command you'll use: cd ~/my_robot_ws colcon build This will: Discover all packages in src/ Determine build order based on dependencies Build each package Install results to install/ Output: Starting >>> my_first_package Finished <<< my_first_package [0.50s] Starting >>> my_second_package Finished <<< my_second_package [0.45s] Summary: 2 packages finished [1.02s]
When you run colcon build, here's what happens: Source Code (src/) ↓ [Build System] ↓ Compiled Code (build/) ↓ [Installation] ↓ Ready to Use (install/)

my_robot_ws/ ├── src/ # Your source code (INPUT) ├── build/ # Temporary build artifacts │ ├── package1/ # Compiled .o files, CMake cache, etc. │ └── package2/ ├── install/ # Final installed packages (OUTPUT) │ ├── package1/ │ ├── package2/ │ └── setup.bash # Source this to use packages └── log/ # Build logs for debugging └── latest_build/ tip After building, you must source the setup script to use your packages: source install/setup.bash
Build specific packages instead of everything:
colcon build --packages-up-to my_package This builds my_package and all packages it depends on (but not packages that depend on it).
Customize your build with these useful flags:

Build multiple packages simultaneously (faster): colcon build --parallel-workers 4 Or use all CPU cores: colcon build --parallel-workers $(nproc) warning More workers = faster builds but more RAM usage. If builds fail with memory errors, reduce workers.

For Python packages, create symlinks instead of copying files: colcon build --symlink-install Benefits: Edit Python code and see changes immediately (no rebuild) Faster builds Saves disk space When to use: During development of Python nodes When iterating quickly on Python code When NOT to use: C++ packages (doesn't work) Before deployment (use regular install)
Keep building even if one package fails: colcon build --continue-on-error

Pass arguments to CMake (for C++ packages): colcon build --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release Build types: Debug: Includes debug symbols, no optimization Release: Optimized, no debug info (faster runtime) RelWithDebInfo: Optimized + debug symbols
See detailed build output: colcon build --event-handlers console_direct+ Useful for: Debugging build failures Understanding what's happening Seeing compiler warnings
Sometimes you need a fresh start:
rm -rf build install log colcon build
rm -rf build/my_package install/my_package colcon build --packages-select my_package tip There's no colcon clean command, so you manually delete the directories.
cd ~/my_robot_ws rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y colcon build --symlink-install source install/setup.bash
# Edit Python code... # No rebuild needed with --symlink-install! source install/setup.bash # Refresh environment ros2 run my_package my_node
# Edit C++ code... colcon build --packages-select my_cpp_package source install/setup.bash ros2 run my_cpp_package my_node
After building, you must source the setup script to use your packages:

To automatically source on every new terminal: echo "source ~/my_robot_ws/install/setup.bash" >> ~/.bashrc warning Be careful with automatic sourcing—it can cause conflicts if you work on multiple workspaces.

Symptom: CMake Error: Could not find package 'geometry_msgs' Diagnosis: Missing dependency Solution: Add to package.xml: <depend>geometry_msgs</depend> Install dependencies: rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y Rebuild: colcon build --packages-select my_package
Symptom: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'my_package.my_node' Diagnosis: Forgot to source setup script Solution: source install/setup.bash ros2 run my_package my_node

Symptom: "Failed" message but no error details Solution: Check the log files: cat log/latest_build/my_package/stdout_stderr.log Or rebuild with verbose output: colcon build --packages-select my_package --event-handlers console_direct+
