For complex projects, you might want different build configurations:
# Create alias alias colcon_debug='colcon build --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug' # Use it colcon_debug
Install ccache: sudo apt install ccache Use it: colcon build --cmake-args -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache

After building, verify packages are available: # List all packages ros2 pkg list # Check specific package ros2 pkg prefix my_package # List executables in package ros2 pkg executables my_package # Try running a node ros2 run my_package my_node

Time different build strategies: # Full rebuild rm -rf build install time colcon build # With parallel workers rm -rf build install time colcon build --parallel-workers $(nproc) # With symlink rm -rf build install time colcon build --symlink-install --parallel-workers $(nproc) Compare the times!

Create a workspace with 3 packages where: package_c depends on package_b package_b depends on package_a Practice: # Build only package_a colcon build --packages-select package_a # Build package_c and its dependencies colcon build --packages-up-to package_c # Build package_a and packages depending on it colcon build --packages-above package_a
Intentionally break a package (remove a dependency from package.xml). Practice: Try to build it Read the error message Check the log file Fix the issue Rebuild successfully

Command Purpose colcon build Build all packages colcon build --packages-select PKG Build specific package colcon build --packages-up-to PKG Build package + dependencies colcon build --symlink-install Use symlinks (Python) colcon build --parallel-workers N Use N parallel jobs colcon test Run tests colcon test-result --all Show test results colcon list List all packages colcon graph Show dependency graph

In this section, you learned: colcon is ROS 2's build tool for multi-package workspaces colcon build compiles and installs packages Selective building speeds up development --symlink-install enables quick Python iterations Always source install/setup.bash after building How to troubleshoot common build errors Build optimization techniques

Now that you can build packages efficiently, let's learn how to launch multiple nodes simultaneously with launch files in 4.4 Launch Files & Multi-Node Systems → Navigation ← Back: 4.2 Dependencies & package.xml Next: 4.4 Launch Files & Multi-Node Systems →

Estimated reading time: 12 minutes Imagine operating a robot that requires 10 different nodes: sensors, motors, navigation, vision, and more. Would you want to open 10 terminals and start each node manually? Of course not! That's where launch files come in—they're scripts that start multiple nodes with a single command. In this section, you'll learn how to create launch files, coordinate multiple nodes, pass parameters, and build complex multi-node robot systems.

Without launch files, starting a robot system looks like this: # Terminal 1 ros2 run robot_sensors camera_node # Terminal 2 ros2 run robot_sensors lidar_node # Terminal 3 ros2 run robot_control motor_controller # Terminal 4 ros2 run robot_brain decision_maker # ... and so on for 10+ nodes With a launch file: ros2 launch robot_bringup robot.launch.py One command starts everything in the correct order with proper configuration!

Convenience: Start multiple nodes with one command Configuration: Set parameters and arguments easily Repeatability: Same setup every time Conditional Logic: Start nodes based on conditions Composition: Include other launch files Documentation: Launch file shows system architecture
ROS 2 uses Python launch files. They're more powerful and flexible than the XML launch files from ROS 1.

Let's create a simple launch file that starts two nodes: # robot_bringup/launch/simple.launch.py from launch import LaunchDescription from launch_ros.actions import Node def generate_launch_description(): return LaunchDescription([ Node( package='demo_nodes_cpp', executable='talker', name='talker' ), Node( package='demo_nodes_cpp', executable='listener', name='listener' ), ]) Structure explained: generate_launch_description(): Required function that returns a LaunchDescription LaunchDescription([...]): Contains list of launch actions Node(...): Launches a ROS 2 node
Add launch files to your package: my_robot_bringup/ ├── package.xml ├── setup.py ├── my_robot_bringup/ │ └── __init__.py └── launch/ # Launch files go here ├── robot.launch.py └── sensors.launch.py

To install launch files, update setup.py: from setuptools import setup import os from glob import glob package_name = 'my_robot_bringup' setup( name=package_name, version='0.0.1', packages=[package_name], data_files=[ ('share/ament_index/resource_index/packages', ['resource/' + package_name]), ('share/' + package_name, ['package.xml']), # Install launch files (os.path.join('share', package_name, 'launch'), glob('launch/*.launch.py')), ], install_requires=['setuptools'], zip_safe=True, maintainer='Your Name', maintainer_email='you@example.com', description='Robot bringup package', license='Apache-2.0', tests_require=['pytest'], )

After building: colcon build --packages-select my_robot_bringup source install/setup.bash # Run from package ros2 launch my_robot_bringup robot.launch.py # Or run directly ros2 launch path/to/robot.launch.py

Node( package='my_package', # Package name executable='my_node', # Node executable name name='custom_node_name', # Override node name namespace='robot1', # Namespace for topics output='screen', # Show output in terminal parameters=[{ 'param1': 42, 'param2': 'hello' }], arguments=['--ros-args', '--log-level', 'debug'], remappings=[ ('/input_topic', '/custom_input') ] )
Control where node output goes: # Show in terminal output='screen' # Hide output output='log' # Custom output output={'stdout': 'screen', 'stderr': 'log'}
Redirect topics: Node( package='sensor_package', executable='camera', remappings=[ ('image', 'camera/image'), # Rename topic ('camera_info', 'camera/camera_info') ] )

Create a YAML file: # config/robot_params.yaml /**: ros__parameters: max_speed: 2.0 min_speed: 0.1 acceleration: 0.5 wheel_radius: 0.05 Load in launch file: import os from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory config = os.path.join( get_package_share_directory('my_robot_bringup'), 'config', 'robot_params.yaml' ) Node( package='my_package', executable='my_node', parameters=[config] )

Accept arguments when launching: from launch import LaunchDescription from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration from launch_ros.actions import Node def generate_launch_description(): # Declare arguments speed_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'max_speed', default_value='1.0', description='Maximum robot speed' ) # Use arguments return LaunchDescription([ speed_arg, Node( package='my_package', executable='my_node', parameters=[{ 'max_speed': LaunchConfiguration('max_speed') }] ) ]) Run with custom argument: ros2 launch my_robot_bringup robot.launch.py max_speed:=2.5

from launch.conditions import IfCondition from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration DeclareLaunchArgument('use_camera', default_value='true'), Node( package='sensor_package', executable='camera_node', condition=IfCondition(LaunchConfiguration('use_camera')) ) Run without camera: ros2 launch my_robot_bringup robot.launch.py use_camera:=false
from launch.conditions import UnlessCondition Node( package='simulation', executable='sim_node', condition=UnlessCondition(LaunchConfiguration('use_real_robot')) )
Include other launch files to build modular systems:

from launch.actions import IncludeLaunchDescription from launch.launch_description_sources import PythonLaunchDescriptionSource from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory import os def generate_launch_description(): sensors_launch = IncludeLaunchDescription( PythonLaunchDescriptionSource([ os.path.join( get_package_share_directory('robot_sensors'), 'launch', 'sensors.launch.py' ) ]) ) return LaunchDescription([ sensors_launch, Node( package='robot_control', executable='controller' ) ])

documents.t: Let's build a complete robot system with multiple nodes:

from launch import LaunchDescription from launch_ros.actions import Node def generate_launch_description(): """Launch all sensor nodes""" return LaunchDescription([ # Camera node Node( package='robot_sensors', executable='camera_node', name='camera', output='screen', parameters=[{ 'frame_rate': 30, 'resolution': '640x480' }] ), # LiDAR node Node( package='robot_sensors', executable='lidar_node', name='lidar', output='screen', parameters=[{ 'scan_rate': 10, 'range_max': 10.0 }] ), # IMU node Node( package='robot_sensors', executable='imu_node', name='imu', output='screen' ), ])

import os from launch import LaunchDescription from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument, IncludeLaunchDescription from launch.conditions import IfCondition from launch.launch_description_sources import PythonLaunchDescriptionSource from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration from launch_ros.actions import Node from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory def generate_launch_description(): # Declare arguments use_sensors = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'use_sensors', default_value='true', description='Whether to launch sensor nodes' ) use_sim = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'sim', default_value='false', description='Whether to use simulation' ) # Get package directories bringup_dir = get_package_share_directory('robot_bringup') # Include sensor launch file sensors_launch = IncludeLaunchDescription( PythonLaunchDescriptionSource([ os.path.join(bringup_dir, 'launch', 'sensors.launch.py') ]), condition=IfCondition(LaunchConfiguration('use_sensors')) ) # Control node controller = Node( package='robot_control', executable='motor_controller', name='controller', output='screen', parameters=[{ 'max_speed': 2.0, 'simulation': LaunchConfiguration('sim') }] ) # Navigation node navigator = Node( package='robot_navigation', executable='path_planner', name='navigator', output='screen' ) # State publisher for robot model robot_state_publisher = Node( package='robot_state_publisher', executable='robot_state_publisher', name='robot_state_publisher', output='screen', parameters=[{ 'robot_description': open( os.path.join(bringup_dir, 'urdf', 'robot.urdf') ).read() }] ) return LaunchDescription([ use_sensors, use_sim, sensors_launch, controller, navigator, robot_state_publisher, ]) Run the full system: # Normal mode with sensors ros2 launch robot_bringup robot_full.launch.py # Simulation mode without sensors ros2 launch robot_bringup robot_full.launch.py sim:=true use_sensors:=false
launch/ ├── sensors.launch.py # All sensors ├── navigation.launch.py # Navigation stack ├── control.launch.py # Motor control └── robot_full.launch.py # Complete system
# BAD Node(package='pkg', executable='node1', name='n1') # GOOD Node( package='robot_sensors', executable='camera_driver', name='front_camera' )

def generate_launch_description(): """ Launch complete robot system. Arguments: sim: Use simulation (default: false) use_sensors: Launch sensor nodes (default: true) """ # Sensor nodes camera = Node(...) # Front-facing camera for vision lidar = Node(...) # 360-degree LiDAR for mapping # ... rest of launch file
DeclareLaunchArgument( 'max_speed', default_value='1.0', # Always provide sensible default description='Maximum robot speed in m/s' )

from launch.actions import OpaqueFunction def validate_and_launch(context): speed = float(LaunchConfiguration('max_speed').perform(context)) if speed < 0 or speed > 5.0: raise ValueError(f"max_speed must be between 0 and 5.0, got {speed}") return [] LaunchDescription([ DeclareLaunchArgument('max_speed'), OpaqueFunction(function=validate_and_launch), # ... nodes ])

ros2 launch robot_bringup robot.launch.py --show-args Output: Arguments (pass arguments as '<name>:=<value>'): 'max_speed': Maximum robot speed in m/s (default: '1.0') 'sim': Use simulation mode (default: 'false')
Add debug prints: from launch.actions import LogInfo LogInfo(msg=['Max speed is: ', LaunchConfiguration('max_speed')])
After launching: ros2 node list ros2 node info /node_name ros2 topic list

# Launch same nodes for multiple robots robot1_nodes = [ Node( package='robot_control', executable='controller', namespace='robot1' ), Node( package='robot_sensors', executable='camera', namespace='robot1' ) ] robot2_nodes = [ Node( package='robot_control', executable='controller', namespace='robot2' ), Node( package='robot_sensors', executable='camera', namespace='robot2' ) ] Topics become /robot1/topic and /robot2/topic.
from launch.actions import GroupAction sensors = GroupAction([ Node(package='sensors', executable='camera'), Node(package='sensors', executable='lidar'), Node(package='sensors', executable='imu'), ])

Run actions when events occur: from launch.actions import RegisterEventHandler, EmitEvent, Shutdown from launch.event_handlers import OnProcessExit shutdown_handler = RegisterEventHandler( OnProcessExit( target_action=critical_node, on_exit=[EmitEvent(event=Shutdown())] ) ) This shuts down everything if a critical node exits.
Create a launch file that starts: Camera node (30 fps) LiDAR node (10 Hz) IMU node (100 Hz) Each with appropriate parameters.
Create a launch file with a use_simulation argument that: If true: launches simulation nodes If false: launches real hardware drivers
Create three launch files: sensors.launch.py - All sensors control.launch.py - Motor controllers full_robot.launch.py - Includes both above Test launching them individually and together.
Create a YAML config file and a launch file that: Loads parameters from YAML Accepts command-line arguments to override specific parameters Prints the final parameter values

When your launch file doesn't work: Check file is in launch/ directory Verify setup.py includes launch files in data_files Rebuild and source: colcon build && source install/setup.bash Check package names are correct: ros2 pkg list Verify executable names: ros2 pkg executables package_name Look for Python syntax errors Check indentation (Python is sensitive!) View launch arguments: --show-args Check node output: output='screen'

Congratulations on making it this far! You've learned ROS 2 concepts, mastered Python nodes, created robot descriptions with URDF, and built packages. Now it's time to put it all together and build something genuinely exciting: a walking gait publisher for a humanoid robot. By the end of this chapter, you'll have a working ROS 2 system that generates walking trajectories for a humanoid robot and visualizes them in RViz. This is not a toy example—this is real robotics engineering that forms the foundation of how actual humanoid robots walk.

Estimated Time 20 minutes Now that we have our package set up, it's time for the exciting part—understanding and implementing the mathematics that makes humanoid robots walk! Don't worry if you're not a math expert; we'll build this up step by step with clear explanations and visualizations.
A gait is the pattern of movement used for locomotion. For humans (and humanoid robots), walking involves a coordinated sequence of leg movements that maintains balance while moving forward.

A complete walking cycle for one leg consists of two phases: Stance Phase (~60% of cycle) The foot is on the ground The leg supports the body weight The hip extends (moves backward relative to the body) The knee is mostly straight The ankle stabilizes the foot Swing Phase (~40% of cycle) The foot is in the air The leg moves forward for the next step The hip flexes (moves forward) The knee bends to clear the ground The ankle prepares for landing Phase Coordination While one leg is in stance phase, the other is in swing phase. They're 180° out of phase—when the left leg is at 0° in its cycle, the right leg is at 180°.

To generate walking motion, we need to define: Step frequency (f): How many steps per second (typically 0.5-1.0 Hz for humanoids) Step height (h): How high the foot lifts during swing (typically 0.05-0.1 m) Stride length (s): How far forward the foot moves (typically 0.1-0.3 m) Joint ranges: Limits on how far each joint can move

We use sinusoidal (sine and cosine) functions for gait generation because: ✅ They produce smooth, continuous motion (no jerky movements) ✅ They're periodic (repeat naturally for continuous walking) ✅ They're differentiable (easy to compute velocities and accelerations) ✅ They're computationally efficient ✅ They approximate biological walking patterns reasonably well

The hip joint controls forward/backward leg motion. During walking: θ_hip(t) = A_hip * sin(2π * f * t + φ) Where: θ_hip: Hip joint angle (radians) A_hip: Amplitude of hip motion (determines stride length) f: Step frequency (Hz) t: Time (seconds) φ: Phase offset (0 for left leg, π for right leg) Physical meaning: The hip swings from negative (leg back) to positive (leg forward) angles.

The knee needs to bend during swing phase to lift the foot. We use a squared sine wave to keep the knee mostly straight during stance: θ_knee(t) = -A_knee * sin²(2π * f * t + φ) Where: θ_knee: Knee joint angle (radians, negative = bent) A_knee: Maximum knee bend angle The squared sine ensures the knee is only bent during swing phase Physical meaning: The knee bends only when the leg is swinging forward, stays straight during stance.

The ankle provides fine control for foot placement: θ_ankle(t) = A_ankle * sin(2π * f * t + φ + ψ) Where: θ_ankle: Ankle joint angle (radians) A_ankle: Ankle motion amplitude (small, for stability) ψ: Additional phase shift for timing Physical meaning: The ankle adjusts foot angle for smooth heel-to-toe motion.

Let's create a Python class that encapsulates all this mathematics. Create a new file: gait_publisher/math/gait_generator.py #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Gait Generator for Humanoid Walking Generates sinusoidal joint trajectories for bipedal walking motion. """ import math from typing import Dict, Tuple class GaitGenerator: """ Generates walking gait trajectories for a bipedal humanoid robot. Uses sinusoidal functions to create smooth, periodic joint motions that approximate natural walking patterns. """ def __init__( self, frequency: float = 0.5, step_height: float = 0.08, stride_length: float = 0.15, ): """ Initialize the gait generator. Args: frequency: Step frequency in Hz (steps per second) step_height: Maximum height foot lifts off ground in meters stride_length: Forward distance of each step in meters """ self.frequency = frequency # Hz self.step_height = step_height # meters self.stride_length = stride_length # meters # Convert physical parameters to joint angles # These are simplified kinematic approximations self.hip_amplitude = self._stride_to_hip_angle(stride_length) self.knee_amplitude = self._step_height_to_knee_angle(step_height) self.ankle_amplitude = 0.1 # Small ankle motion for stability # Phase offsets self.left_phase = 0.0 # Left leg starts at 0 self.right_phase = math.pi # Right leg 180° out of phase def _stride_to_hip_angle(self, stride: float) -> float: """ Convert stride length to hip joint amplitude. Simplified kinematic approximation: For a leg length of ~0.8m, hip angle ≈ arcsin(stride / leg_length) Args: stride: Stride length in meters Returns: Hip amplitude in radians """ leg_length = 0.8 # Approximate total leg length # Use small angle approximation for simplicity return stride / leg_length def _step_height_to_knee_angle(self, height: float) -> float: """ Convert step height to knee joint amplitude. When knee bends, foot lifts. Approximate relationship: height ≈ thigh_length * (1 - cos(knee_angle)) For our robot: thigh ≈ 0.4m Args: height: Step height in meters Returns: Knee amplitude in radians """ thigh_length = 0.4 # Solve for knee angle if height >= 2 * thigh_length: # Can't lift that high! return math.pi / 2 return math.acos(1 - height / thigh_length) def get_joint_angles(self, time: float) -> Dict[str, float]: """ Compute all joint angles at a given time. Args: time: Current time in seconds Returns: Dictionary mapping joint names to angles in radians """ # Compute phase for current time phase = 2 * math.pi * self.frequency * time # Left leg joints left_hip = self._hip_trajectory(phase, self.left_phase) left_knee = self._knee_trajectory(phase, self.left_phase) left_ankle = self._ankle_trajectory(phase, self.left_phase) # Right leg joints (180° out of phase) right_hip = self._hip_trajectory(phase, self.right_phase) right_knee = self._knee_trajectory(phase, self.right_phase) right_ankle = self._ankle_trajectory(phase, self.right_phase) return { 'left_hip_joint': left_hip, 'left_knee_joint': left_knee, 'left_ankle_joint': left_ankle, 'right_hip_joint': right_hip, 'right_knee_joint': right_knee, 'right_ankle_joint': right_ankle, } def _hip_trajectory(self, phase: float, offset: float) -> float: """ Compute hip joint angle. Uses sine wave for smooth forward/backward motion. Positive angle = leg forward, Negative = leg back Args: phase: Current phase in radians offset: Phase offset for this leg Returns: Hip angle in radians """ return self.hip_amplitude * math.sin(phase + offset) def _knee_trajectory(self, phase: float, offset: float) -> float: """ Compute knee joint angle. Uses squared sine wave to bend knee only during swing phase. Negative angle = knee bent Args: phase: Current phase in radians offset: Phase offset for this leg Returns: Knee angle in radians (negative) """ # Squared sine: only positive during swing phase sin_val = math.sin(phase + offset) return -self.knee_amplitude * (sin_val ** 2) def _ankle_trajectory(self, phase: float, offset: float) -> float: """ Compute ankle joint angle. Small sinusoidal motion for foot angle control. Args: phase: Current phase in radians offset: Phase offset for this leg Returns: Ankle angle in radians """ # Add small phase shift for proper timing with hip/knee return self.ankle_amplitude * math.sin(phase + offset + math.pi / 4) def set_parameters( self, frequency: float = None, step_height: float = None, stride_length: float = None ): """ Update gait parameters dynamically. Args: frequency: New step frequency (Hz) step_height: New step height (meters) stride_length: New stride length (meters) """ if frequency is not None: self.frequency = frequency if step_height is not None: self.step_height = step_height self.knee_amplitude = self._step_height_to_knee_angle(step_height) if stride_length is not None: self.stride_length = stride_length self.hip_amplitude = self._stride_to_hip_angle(stride_length) def get_parameters(self) -> Dict[str, float]: """ Get current gait parameters. Returns: Dictionary of current parameters """ return { 'frequency': self.frequency, 'step_height': self.step_height, 'stride_length': self.stride_length, 'hip_amplitude': self.hip_amplitude, 'knee_amplitude': self.knee_amplitude, 'ankle_amplitude': self.ankle_amplitude, }
Let's break down the key components:

def __init__(self, frequency=0.5, step_height=0.08, stride_length=0.15): We initialize with physical parameters (frequency, height, distance) that are intuitive to understand, then convert them to joint angles internally.

def _stride_to_hip_angle(self, stride: float) -> float: leg_length = 0.8 return stride / leg_length This converts "I want to step 15cm forward" to "The hip needs to rotate X radians." This is a simplified kinematic model—real robots use more complex inverse kinematics.
Each joint has its own trajectory function: Hip: Simple sine wave for smooth oscillation Knee: Squared sine to bend only during swing Ankle: Sine with phase shift for timing
self.left_phase = 0.0 self.right_phase = math.pi # 180° out of phase This ensures that when the left leg is forward, the right is back, and vice versa.

documents.t: Excellent work! You've implemented the mathematical foundation for walking gaits. You now have a GaitGenerator class that can compute joint angles for smooth, coordinated walking motion. In the next section, we'll integrate this generator with ROS 2 by creating a publisher node that sends these joint commands at real-time control rates (50 Hz). This is where your gait generator becomes a working ROS 2 system!
← Previous: 5.1 Project Setup | Next: 5.3 Publisher Node → Chapter 5 Sections: 5.1 Project Setup 5.2 Gait Mathematics (You are here) 5.3 Publisher Node 5.4 Visualization & Testing

Estimated Time 15 minutes Now for the exciting part—bringing our gait generator into the ROS 2 ecosystem! In this section, we'll create a publisher node that sends joint commands at real-time control frequencies. This is where your mathematical trajectories become actual robot motion.

Our publisher node will: Create a GaitGenerator instance with configurable parameters Set up a timer that triggers at 50 Hz (every 20 milliseconds) Compute joint angles at each timer tick using the gait generator Publish JointState messages containing all joint positions Support dynamic reconfiguration through ROS 2 parameters

Real-time robot control typically operates at 50-200 Hz. We're using 50 Hz because: ✅ Fast enough for smooth motion visualization ✅ Matches common robot control frequencies ✅ Provides 20ms update intervals (responsive) ✅ Not too demanding on CPU resources

Before we write code, let's understand the message type we'll publish: ros2 interface show sensor_msgs/msg/JointState You'll see: std_msgs/Header header string[] name # Joint names float64[] position # Joint positions in radians float64[] velocity # Joint velocities (optional) float64[] effort # Joint efforts/torques (optional) For our gait publisher, we'll populate: header: Timestamp for synchronization name: List of our 6 joint names position: The computed angles from our gait generator

Let's create the main publisher node: gait_publisher/gait_publisher_node.py #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Gait Publisher Node for Humanoid Walking Publishes joint state trajectories for bipedal walking motion. Uses the GaitGenerator to compute smooth, periodic joint angles. """ import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from sensor_msgs.msg import JointState from rcl_interfaces.msg import ParameterDescriptor from gait_publisher.math.gait_generator import GaitGenerator class GaitPublisherNode(Node): """ ROS 2 node that publishes walking gait trajectories. This node generates and publishes JointState messages at a fixed control frequency (50 Hz by default), enabling visualization and simulation of humanoid walking motion. """ def __init__(self): super().__init__('gait_publisher') # Declare parameters with descriptions self.declare_parameter( 'publish_frequency', 50.0, ParameterDescriptor(description='Joint state publish frequency (Hz)') ) self.declare_parameter( 'step_frequency', 0.5, ParameterDescriptor(description='Walking step frequency (Hz)') ) self.declare_parameter( 'step_height', 0.08, ParameterDescriptor(description='Step height in meters') ) self.declare_parameter( 'stride_length', 0.15, ParameterDescriptor(description='Stride length in meters') ) # Get parameter values self.publish_freq = self.get_parameter('publish_frequency').value step_freq = self.get_parameter('step_frequency').value step_height = self.get_parameter('step_height').value stride_length = self.get_parameter('stride_length').value # Create gait generator self.gait_generator = GaitGenerator( frequency=step_freq, step_height=step_height, stride_length=stride_length ) # Create publisher self.joint_pub = self.create_publisher( JointState, 'joint_states', 10 # Queue size ) # Define joint names (must match URDF!) self.joint_names = [ 'left_hip_joint', 'left_knee_joint', 'left_ankle_joint', 'right_hip_joint', 'right_knee_joint', 'right_ankle_joint', ] # Create timer for periodic publishing timer_period = 1.0 / self.publish_freq # seconds self.timer = self.create_timer(timer_period, self.timer_callback) # Initialize time tracking self.start_time = self.get_clock().now() # Log startup information self.get_logger().info('Gait Publisher Node started') self.get_logger().info(f'Publishing at {self.publish_freq} Hz') self.get_logger().info(f'Step frequency: {step_freq} Hz') self.get_logger().info(f'Step height: {step_height} m') self.get_logger().info(f'Stride length: {stride_length} m') def timer_callback(self): """ Timer callback that computes and publishes joint states. Called at the publish frequency (default 50 Hz). Computes current joint angles and publishes them. """ # Calculate elapsed time since start current_time = self.get_clock().now() elapsed = (current_time - self.start_time).nanoseconds / 1e9 # Convert to seconds # Get joint angles from gait generator joint_angles = self.gait_generator.get_joint_angles(elapsed) # Create and populate JointState message msg = JointState() msg.header.stamp = current_time.to_msg() msg.header.frame_id = '' # Not needed for joint states msg.name = self.joint_names msg.position = [ joint_angles['left_hip_joint'], joint_angles['left_knee_joint'], joint_angles['left_ankle_joint'], joint_angles['right_hip_joint'], joint_angles['right_knee_joint'], joint_angles['right_ankle_joint'], ] # Velocities and efforts are optional; we'll leave them empty msg.velocity = [] msg.effort = [] # Publish the message self.joint_pub.publish(msg) def update_gait_parameters(self): """ Update gait generator with current parameter values. This allows dynamic reconfiguration while the node is running. """ step_freq = self.get_parameter('step_frequency').value step_height = self.get_parameter('step_height').value stride_length = self.get_parameter('stride_length').value self.gait_generator.set_parameters( frequency=step_freq, step_height=step_height, stride_length=stride_length ) self.get_logger().info('Gait parameters updated') def main(args=None): """Main entry point for the gait publisher node.""" rclpy.init(args=args) node = GaitPublisherNode() try: rclpy.spin(node) except KeyboardInterrupt: pass finally: node.get_logger().info('Shutting down gait publisher') node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == '__main__': main()
Let's break down the key components:
self.declare_parameter('publish_frequency', 50.0) We declare parameters that can be: Set via command line: --ros-args -p step_height:=0.10 Set in launch files Changed at runtime with ros2 param set
timer_period = 1.0 / self.publish_freq # 50 Hz = 0.02 seconds self.timer = self.create_timer(timer_period, self.timer_callback) This creates a timer that calls timer_callback every 20ms (for 50 Hz).
elapsed = (current_time - self.start_time).nanoseconds / 1e9 We track elapsed time to pass to the gait generator. This ensures smooth, continuous motion.
msg.name = self.joint_names msg.position = [joint_angles['left_hip_joint'], ...] We create a JointState message with names matching our URDF and positions from the gait generator.

documents.t: Launch files make starting your system easy. Let's create one: launch/gait_publisher.launch.py #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Launch file for the gait publisher node. This launch file starts the gait publisher with configurable parameters. """ from launch import LaunchDescription from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration from launch_ros.actions import Node def generate_launch_description(): """Generate launch description for gait publisher.""" # Declare launch arguments step_frequency_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'step_frequency', default_value='0.5', description='Walking step frequency in Hz' ) step_height_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'step_height', default_value='0.08', description='Step height in meters' ) stride_length_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'stride_length', default_value='0.15', description='Stride length in meters' ) publish_frequency_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'publish_frequency', default_value='50.0', description='Joint state publish frequency in Hz' ) # Create the gait publisher node gait_publisher_node = Node( package='gait_publisher', executable='gait_publisher_node', name='gait_publisher', output='screen', parameters=[{ 'step_frequency': LaunchConfiguration('step_frequency'), 'step_height': LaunchConfiguration('step_height'), 'stride_length': LaunchConfiguration('stride_length'), 'publish_frequency': LaunchConfiguration('publish_frequency'), }] ) return LaunchDescription([ step_frequency_arg, step_height_arg, stride_length_arg, publish_frequency_arg, gait_publisher_node, ]) This launch file: Defines configurable arguments with defaults Creates the gait publisher node with those parameters Outputs logs to the screen

Let's build and test our publisher: # Navigate to workspace root cd ~/humanoid_ws # Build the package colcon build --packages-select gait_publisher # Source the workspace source install/setup.bash # Run the node directly ros2 run gait_publisher gait_publisher_node You should see: [INFO] [gait_publisher]: Gait Publisher Node started [INFO] [gait_publisher]: Publishing at 50.0 Hz [INFO] [gait_publisher]: Step frequency: 0.5 Hz [INFO] [gait_publisher]: Step height: 0.08 m [INFO] [gait_publisher]: Stride length: 0.15 m

In a new terminal, check that joint states are being published: # Source your workspace source ~/humanoid_ws/install/setup.bash # Echo the joint states topic ros2 topic echo /joint_states --once You should see output like: header: stamp: sec: 1234567890 nanosec: 123456789 frame_id: '' name: - left_hip_joint - left_knee_joint - left_ankle_joint - right_hip_joint - right_knee_joint - right_ankle_joint position: - 0.0234567 - -0.0123456 - 0.0012345 - -0.0234567 - -0.0123456 - -0.0012345 velocity: [] effort: []
Verify the publishing frequency: ros2 topic hz /joint_states You should see: average rate: 50.000 min: 0.020s max: 0.020s std dev: 0.00001s window: 50

Now test with the launch file: # Launch with default parameters ros2 launch gait_publisher gait_publisher.launch.py # Or launch with custom parameters ros2 launch gait_publisher gait_publisher.launch.py step_frequency:=0.8 step_height:=0.10

For easy configuration, let's create a YAML parameter file: config/gait_params.yaml gait_publisher: ros__parameters: # Publishing configuration publish_frequency: 50.0 # Hz # Gait parameters step_frequency: 0.5 # Hz (steps per second) step_height: 0.08 # meters stride_length: 0.15 # meters # Alternative configurations for different gaits # Fast walk # step_frequency: 0.8 # step_height: 0.06 # stride_length: 0.20 # Slow walk # step_frequency: 0.3 # step_height: 0.10 # stride_length: 0.10 # March (high steps) # step_frequency: 0.4 # step_height: 0.15 # stride_length: 0.08 Update the launch file to use this config: launch/gait_publisher.launch.py #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Launch file for the gait publisher node with parameter file support. """ from launch import LaunchDescription from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration from launch_ros.actions import Node from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory import os def generate_launch_description(): """Generate launch description for gait publisher.""" # Get package directory pkg_share = get_package_share_directory('gait_publisher') params_file = os.path.join(pkg_share, 'config', 'gait_params.yaml') # Declare launch arguments use_params_file_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'use_params_file', default_value='true', description='Whether to use parameter file or launch arguments' ) step_frequency_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'step_frequency', default_value='0.5', description='Walking step frequency in Hz' ) step_height_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'step_height', default_value='0.08', description='Step height in meters' ) stride_length_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'stride_length', default_value='0.15', description='Stride length in meters' ) # Create the gait publisher node gait_publisher_node = Node( package='gait_publisher', executable='gait_publisher_node', name='gait_publisher', output='screen', parameters=[params_file] # Load from YAML file ) return LaunchDescription([ use_params_file_arg, step_frequency_arg, step_height_arg, stride_length_arg, gait_publisher_node, ])

Estimated Time 15 minutes This is it—the moment you've been building toward! In this final section, we'll bring your humanoid to life in RViz. You'll see your mathematical trajectories transform into actual walking motion. Let's make your robot walk!

To visualize our walking humanoid, we need three components working together: URDF Model → Defines the robot's structure (already done!) Joint States → Provides current joint positions (your gait publisher!) Robot State Publisher → Transforms joint states into 3D poses RViz → Visualizes the robot in 3D Here's the data flow: GaitPublisher → /joint_states → RobotStatePublisher → /tf → RViz What is robot_state_publisher? robot_state_publisher subscribes to /joint_states, reads your URDF, and publishes transformations (/tf) that represent where each link is in 3D space. This is what makes your robot model move in RViz!

Let's create a launch file that brings everything together: launch/display_walking.launch.py #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Complete launch file for visualizing walking humanoid in RViz. This launch file starts: 1. robot_state_publisher (with URDF) 2. gait_publisher_node (joint trajectory generator) 3. RViz (with custom configuration) """ import os from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory from launch import LaunchDescription from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration, Command from launch_ros.actions import Node def generate_launch_description(): """Generate the launch description for walking visualization.""" # Get package directories pkg_share = get_package_share_directory('gait_publisher') # File paths urdf_file = os.path.join(pkg_share, 'urdf', 'simple_humanoid.urdf') rviz_config_file = os.path.join(pkg_share, 'config', 'walking_viz.rviz') params_file = os.path.join(pkg_share, 'config', 'gait_params.yaml') # Declare launch arguments use_sim_time_arg = DeclareLaunchArgument( 'use_sim_time', default_value='false', description='Use simulation time' ) # Read URDF file with open(urdf_file, 'r') as infp: robot_description = infp.read() # Robot State Publisher Node # This node publishes the robot's state based on URDF and joint states robot_state_publisher_node = Node( package='robot_state_publisher', executable='robot_state_publisher', name='robot_state_publisher', output='screen', parameters=[{ 'robot_description': robot_description, 'use_sim_time': LaunchConfiguration('use_sim_time') }] ) # Gait Publisher Node # This node generates and publishes walking joint trajectories gait_publisher_node = Node( package='gait_publisher', executable='gait_publisher_node', name='gait_publisher', output='screen', parameters=[params_file] ) # RViz Node # Visualization tool rviz_node = Node( package='rviz2', executable='rviz2', name='rviz2', output='screen', arguments=['-d', rviz_config_file] if os.path.exists(rviz_config_file) else [] ) return LaunchDescription([ use_sim_time_arg, robot_state_publisher_node, gait_publisher_node, rviz_node, ])

Let's rebuild and launch the complete system: # Navigate to workspace root cd ~/humanoid_ws # Build colcon build --packages-select gait_publisher # Source source install/setup.bash # Launch the complete visualization ros2 launch gait_publisher display_walking.launch.py
When RViz opens, you should see:
Grid: A reference grid on the floor Robot model: Your humanoid standing upright TF frames: Coordinate frames for each link

Within a few seconds, you should see: ✅ Legs alternating: Left forward when right is back ✅ Knees bending: During swing phase (leg forward motion) ✅ Smooth motion: No jerky or discontinuous movements ✅ Periodic pattern: Motion repeats every 2 seconds (at 0.5 Hz) What to Look For Watch the feet! You should see them lifting off the ground during swing and staying relatively stationary during stance. The motion should look like walking in place.
Optimize your view with these camera controls:
Left-click + drag: Orbit around the robot Middle-click + drag: Pan the view Right-click + drag: Zoom in/out Scroll wheel: Zoom in/out

Orbit to view from the side (sagittal plane) Zoom to see the full robot Set focal point at robot's center of mass You can also view from: Front: See left-right leg coordination Top: See leg positions from above Isometric: 45° angle showing 3D motion

Let's verify that our gait is correct. Open a new terminal: source ~/humanoid_ws/install/setup.bash # Monitor joint state messages ros2 topic echo /joint_states --field name,position You should see periodic values like: name: - left_hip_joint - left_knee_joint - left_ankle_joint - right_hip_joint - right_knee_joint - right_ankle_joint position: - 0.0234567 - -0.0456789 - 0.0012345 - -0.0234567 - -0.0456789 - -0.0012345

✅ Hip values opposite: Left and right hips should have opposite signs ✅ Knee values negative: Knees bend backward (negative angles) ✅ Values changing: Should update 50 times per second ✅ Smooth transitions: No sudden jumps in values

Welcome to Module 2! In this module, we explore digital twins – virtual replicas of physical robots that allow us to simulate, test, and validate robotic systems before deploying them in the real world.

A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical system that mirrors its behavior, physics, and sensor data. For robotics, digital twins enable safe, cost-effective development and testing in simulated environments.

In this module, we will cover: Gazebo Simulation: Setting up Gazebo Ignition/Harmonic for physics-accurate simulation URDF to SDF Conversion: Transforming robot models for simulation Sensor Simulation: Implementing LiDAR, depth cameras, and IMUs in simulation Unity Integration: Using Unity for high-fidelity visualization and human-robot interaction Practical Application: Creating a realistic apartment environment with sensor streaming

By the end of this module, you will be able to: Set up and configure Gazebo for humanoid robot simulation Convert URDF robot models to SDF format Simulate realistic sensors (LiDAR, cameras, IMU) Integrate Unity for photorealistic visualization Create custom simulation environments Stream and visualize sensor data from your digital twin Successfully spin up a complete humanoid digital twin in under 30 minutes

Simulation is essential for robotics. You need to test before deploying to real robots. Gazebo provides this testing ground. Gazebo is a 3D robot simulator. It simulates physics. It simulates sensors. It visualizes robots in 3D. Companies like Boston Dynamics use it. Research labs use it. Now you will too. By the end, you'll have Gazebo running. You'll understand physics configuration. You'll be ready to simulate humanoid robots.

Gazebo simulates the real world. It calculates forces. It detects collisions. It renders sensors. All in real-time. Think of it as a video game engine for robots. But instead of entertainment, it tests robot behavior. You can break things safely.

Type: Scenario Context: You program a walking gait for your humanoid. You want to test it. Explanation: Without simulation, you deploy to the real robot. The gait has a bug. The robot falls. It breaks. Repair costs $500. With simulation, you test in Gazebo first. The robot falls in simulation. No damage. You fix the bug. You test again. It walks perfectly. Then you deploy to the real robot. It works. No damage. No repair costs. Takeaway: Simulation lets you fail safely. Test in the virtual world before the real world.

Gazebo has two major versions: Gazebo Classic (old): Version 11 and earlier No longer recommended Limited features Gazebo (new): Also called Gazebo Harmonic Modern architecture Better physics We use this version Always use the newest Gazebo. Not Gazebo Classic.
First, update your system: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y This ensures all packages are current.

Gazebo isn't in the default Ubuntu repos. Add it: # Library: Gazebo Harmonic (osrf/gazebo latest) # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: Ubuntu 22.04 sudo apt-get install lsb-release wget gnupg sudo wget https://packages.osrfoundation.org/gazebo.gpg -O /usr/share/keyrings/pkgs-osrf-archive-keyring.gpg echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/pkgs-osrf-archive-keyring.gpg] http://packages.osrfoundation.org/gazebo/ubuntu-stable $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gazebo-stable.list > /dev/null This adds the official Gazebo repository.
Now install: sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install gz-harmonic -y This downloads and installs Gazebo. It takes 5-10 minutes.
Check it works: gz sim --version You should see version information. Something like "Gazebo Harmonic 8.0.0".
Try launching Gazebo: gz sim A window appears. This is Gazebo. You see an empty world. Success! Close it with Ctrl+C in the terminal.
Gazebo doesn't calculate physics itself. It uses physics engines. Different engines have different strengths.

ODE (Open Dynamics Engine): Default engine Fast Good enough for most robots Simple to configure Bullet: Better collision detection Used in games Good for complex environments DART: Best for humanoid robots Handles contacts well More accurate Slightly slower Simbody: Very accurate Used for biomechanics Overkill for most projects
For humanoid robots, use DART. It handles foot contacts better. It's more stable for walking. For wheeled robots, use ODE. It's faster.

Type: Comparison Context: You're simulating a bipedal walker. It keeps falling over. Explanation: With ODE, the foot contacts are unstable. The robot jitters. It falls. With DART, contacts are stable. The robot stands firmly. It walks smoothly. DART costs 10% more CPU time. But the accuracy is worth it. Your robot doesn't fall randomly. Takeaway: Choose the right physics engine for your robot type. Humanoids need DART.
Gazebo worlds are defined in SDF files. SDF means Simulation Description Format. It's XML.

Here's a minimal world: worlds/empty_world.sdf <!-- Library: Gazebo Harmonic SDF 1.9 Last updated: 2025-12-05 Tested on: Gazebo Harmonic 8.0 --> <?xml version="1.0"?> <sdf version="1.9"> <world name="empty_world"> <!-- Physics engine --> <physics name="physics" type="dart"> <max_step_size>0.001</max_step_size> <real_time_factor>1.0</real_time_factor> <real_time_update_rate>1000</real_time_update_rate> </physics> <!-- Required plugins --> <plugin filename="gz-sim-physics-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Physics"> </plugin> <plugin filename="gz-sim-user-commands-system" name="gz::sim::systems::UserCommands"> </plugin> <plugin filename="gz-sim-scene-broadcaster-system" name="gz::sim::systems::SceneBroadcaster"> </plugin> <!-- Lighting --> <light type="directional" name="sun"> <pose>0 0 10 0 0 0</pose> <diffuse>0.8 0.8 0.8 1</diffuse> <specular>0.2 0.2 0.2 1</specular> <direction>-0.5 0.1 -0.9</direction> </light> <!-- Ground plane --> <model name="ground"> <static>true</static> <link name="link"> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <plane> <normal>0 0 1</normal> </plane> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <plane> <normal>0 0 1</normal> <size>100 100</size> </plane> </geometry> </visual> </link> </model> </world> </sdf> This creates an empty world. It has physics. It has lighting. It has a ground plane.
Save the file. Then launch it: gz sim empty_world.sdf You see your world. An infinite ground plane. Light from above.
Physics parameters affect simulation quality. Wrong parameters cause instability. Right parameters make simulations stable.

This is critical. Smaller steps are more accurate. But slower. <max_step_size>0.001</max_step_size> This means 1 millisecond per step. 1000 steps per simulated second. For humanoid robots: Use 0.001 (1ms). Smaller is better. For wheeled robots: Use 0.005 (5ms). Faster simulation.

This controls simulation speed: <real_time_factor>1.0</real_time_factor> 1.0 means real-time. 1 simulated second = 1 real second. 0.5 means half speed. Slower than real-time. 2.0 means double speed. Faster than real-time.
How often physics calculates: <real_time_update_rate>1000</real_time_update_rate> 1000 Hz means 1000 updates per second. This matches the 0.001 step size. Always set this to 1.0 / max_step_size.
Contacts are where objects touch. Feet on ground. Hands on objects. These need careful tuning.

Friction prevents sliding: <friction> <ode> <mu>1.0</mu> <mu2>1.0</mu2> </ode> </friction> mu is friction coefficient. 1.0 is like rubber on concrete. 0.1 is like ice. For humanoid feet, use 1.0. High friction prevents slipping.

How "hard" contacts are: <contact> <ode> <kp>1e7</kp> <kd>1.0</kd> </ode> </contact> kp is stiffness. Higher = harder contacts. Lower = softer. For rigid robots, use 1e7 (10 million). kd is damping. It prevents bouncing.

Control how objects bounce: <bounce> <restitution_coefficient>0.0</restitution_coefficient> </bounce> 0.0 = no bounce. Objects stay on ground. 1.0 = perfect bounce. Like a super ball. For walking robots, use 0.0. No bouncing.

Gazebo and ROS 2 need to communicate. Install the bridge: # Library: ros-gz-bridge (ROS 2 Humble) # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Gazebo Harmonic sudo apt-get install ros-humble-ros-gz -y This installs ros_gz packages. They bridge Gazebo to ROS 2.

Start the bridge: ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge /clock@rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock[gz.msgs.Clock This bridges the /clock topic. Gazebo time flows to ROS 2. You can bridge any topic. Sensors. Commands. States.
gz sim Gazebo opens. You see the GUI.
Look at the bottom right. You see "Real Time Factor". It should be close to 1.00. If it's below 0.5, your computer is slow. Or your world is too complex.
In Gazebo, click the top menu. Insert → Model. Select "Box". A box appears. It falls to the ground. Physics works!
In another terminal: ros2 topic list You should see /clock. The bridge works.
Problem: "Error: cannot open display" Solutions: Check you're using a graphical environment Not SSH without X forwarding Try: export DISPLAY=:0
Problem: Gazebo opens but shows black. Solutions: Update GPU drivers For NVIDIA: sudo ubuntu-drivers autoinstall Reboot after driver update
Problem: Real-time factor is 0.1 or lower. Solutions: Increase max_step_size to 0.005 Simplify your robot model Reduce sensor update rates Close other programs
Problem: Robot vibrates violently and flies apart. Solutions: Decrease max_step_size to 0.0005 Increase solver iterations Check your URDF for errors Verify mass values are realistic
Don't load complex worlds immediately. Start empty. Add objects one by one. Test each addition.
Always check real-time factor. Keep it above 0.8. If it drops, simplify your simulation.
Create world files for different scenarios. Testing. Training. Deployment. Each gets its own file.
Put your SDF files in git. Track changes. Revert mistakes easily.

You have a robot model. It's in URDF format. ROS 2 uses it. But Gazebo needs SDF format. You need to convert. This chapter shows you how. You'll learn the differences. You'll convert models. You'll fix common problems. By the end, your robot runs in Gazebo. Perfectly.

URDF was created for ROS. It describes robots simply. It works great with ROS tools. Advantages: Simple structure ROS-native Xacro support Wide adoption Limitations: ROS-specific Limited simulation features No world modeling

SDF was created for Gazebo. It's more powerful. It handles complex simulations. Advantages: Rich simulation features World and environment support Advanced physics Better sensors Limitations: More complex Less ROS integration

Type: Comparison Context: You have a humanoid robot. You want to use it in both ROS 2 and Gazebo. Explanation: Keep your master model in URDF. Use it for ROS 2 tools. Robot state publisher. MoveIt. Everything ROS. Then convert to SDF for Gazebo simulation. SDF handles physics better. It simulates sensors accurately. It models environments. Use both formats. Each for its strength. Takeaway: URDF for ROS integration. SDF for simulation. Convert between them as needed.
URDF files describe robots in XML. Key elements:

Links are rigid bodies: <link name="torso"> <visual> <geometry> <box size="0.3 0.2 0.4"/> </geometry> </visual> <collision> <geometry> <box size="0.3 0.2 0.4"/> </geometry> </collision> <inertial> <mass value="5.0"/> <inertia ixx="0.1" iyy="0.1" izz="0.1" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> </link> This defines a torso. It has visual geometry. Collision geometry. Mass properties.

Joints connect links: <joint name="left_hip" type="revolute"> <parent link="torso"/> <child link="left_thigh"/> <origin xyz="0 0.1 -0.2" rpy="0 0 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> <limit lower="-1.57" upper="1.57" effort="100" velocity="2.0"/> </joint> This connects the torso to left thigh. It rotates. It has limits.
SDF is similar but more detailed:

<link name="torso"> <pose>0 0 0 0 0 0</pose> <inertial> <mass>5.0</mass> <inertia> <ixx>0.1</ixx> <iyy>0.1</iyy> <izz>0.1</izz> <ixy>0</ixy> <ixz>0</ixz> <iyz>0</iyz> </inertia> </inertial> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <box> <size>0.3 0.2 0.4</size> </box> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <box> <size>0.3 0.2 0.4</size> </box> </geometry> </visual> </link> Notice the differences. Each element has a name. Syntax is slightly different.

<joint name="left_hip" type="revolute"> <parent>torso</parent> <child>left_thigh</child> <pose>0 0.1 -0.2 0 0 0</pose> <axis> <xyz>0 1 0</xyz> <limit> <lower>-1.57</lower> <upper>1.57</upper> <effort>100</effort> <velocity>2.0</velocity> </limit> </axis> </joint> The structure is nested differently. The axis contains limits.

Gazebo includes a converter: # Library: Gazebo Harmonic (gz command) # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: Gazebo Harmonic 8.0 gz sdf -p your_robot.urdf > your_robot.sdf This converts automatically. It handles most cases.

If using Xacro: # Process Xacro to URDF ros2 run xacro xacro your_robot.urdf.xacro > temp.urdf # Convert to SDF gz sdf -p temp.urdf > your_robot.sdf # Clean up rm temp.urdf This is a two-step process.

Automate the process: convert_robot.py # Library: subprocess (Python stdlib) # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: Python 3.10, Gazebo Harmonic #!/usr/bin/env python3 import subprocess import sys def convert_to_sdf(urdf_file, sdf_file): """Convert URDF to SDF""" try: result = subprocess.run( ['gz', 'sdf', '-p', urdf_file], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True ) with open(sdf_file, 'w') as f: f.write(result.stdout) print(f"✓ Converted {urdf_file} to {sdf_file}") return True except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e: print(f"✗ Error: {e.stderr}") return False if __name__ == "__main__": if len(sys.argv) != 3: print("Usage: convert_robot.py input.urdf output.sdf") sys.exit(1) urdf_file = sys.argv[1] sdf_file = sys.argv[2] if convert_to_sdf(urdf_file, sdf_file): sys.exit(0) else: sys.exit(1) Save this script. Use it repeatedly.

Type: Decision Guide Context: You have multiple robot variants. You update them frequently. Explanation: Manual conversion is tedious. You convert. You test. You change the URDF. You convert again. This wastes time. Use the script instead. One command converts any robot. Update your URDF. Run the script. Done. Even better, add it to your build process. Every time you build, the SDF updates automatically. Takeaway: Automate repetitive tasks. Scripts save time and prevent errors.
URDF uses attributes: <box size="1 2 3"/> SDF uses elements: <box> <size>1 2 3</size> </box>
URDF uses origin: <origin xyz="1 2 3" rpy="0 0 0"/> SDF uses pose: <pose>1 2 3 0 0 0</pose>

gz sim your_robot.sdf The robot appears. Check these things: Visual Check: Robot looks correct Links are positioned right Colors and textures work Physics Check: Robot doesn't fall through ground Joints move properly No violent explosions Performance Check: Simulation runs smoothly Real-time factor near 1.0
Move joints manually. In Gazebo GUI: Right-click the robot Select "View Joints" Move sliders Joints should move smoothly. No jitter. No instability.
Add objects to the world. Make the robot touch them. Collisions should work correctly.

Symptoms: Robot spawns and immediately falls. Causes: Missing collision geometry Incorrect contact parameters Wrong spawn height Solutions: Check collisions exist: <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <box> <size>0.3 0.2 0.4</size> </box> </geometry> </collision> Set proper spawn height: <pose>0 0 1.0 0 0 0</pose> 1 meter above ground. The robot falls safely.

Symptoms: Parts fly apart violently. Causes: Wrong inertial values Overlapping collision geometry Too-small time step Solutions: Check mass is realistic: <mass>5.0</mass> Not 0.001. Not 10000. Human-scale robots: 1-100 kg. Check inertia values: <inertia> <ixx>0.1</ixx> <iyy>0.1</iyy> <izz>0.1</izz> </inertia> Use realistic values. Don't set to zero.

Symptoms: Joints don't move at all. Causes: Missing axis definition Static model Wrong joint type Solutions: Ensure model is dynamic: <static>false</static> Check axis is defined: <axis> <xyz>0 1 0</xyz> </axis> Verify joint type: <joint name="knee" type="revolute"> Not fixed if you want movement.

Symptoms: Parts are invisible or wrong color. Causes: Wrong mesh paths Missing mesh files Incorrect file format Solutions: Use relative paths: <mesh> <uri>model://my_robot/meshes/torso.stl</uri> </mesh> Or absolute paths: <mesh> <uri>file:///path/to/torso.stl</uri> </mesh> Check file exists: ls /path/to/torso.stl

Improve foot-ground contact: <collision name="foot_collision"> <geometry> <box> <size>0.1 0.05 0.02</size> </box> </geometry> <surface> <friction> <ode> <mu>1.0</mu> <mu2>1.0</mu2> </ode> </friction> <contact> <ode> <kp>1e7</kp> <kd>1.0</kd> </ode> </contact> </surface> </collision> High friction prevents slipping. Stiff contact prevents sinking.

Add damping for stability: <joint name="knee" type="revolute"> <axis> <dynamics> <damping>0.7</damping> <friction>0.1</friction> </dynamics> </axis> </joint> Damping slows oscillations. Friction resists movement.

Here's a minimal humanoid in SDF: simple_humanoid.sdf <!-- Library: Gazebo Harmonic SDF 1.9 Last updated: 2025-12-05 Tested on: Gazebo Harmonic 8.0 --> <?xml version="1.0"?> <sdf version="1.9"> <model name="simple_humanoid"> <pose>0 0 1.0 0 0 0</pose> <static>false</static> <!-- Torso --> <link name="torso"> <inertial> <mass>10.0</mass> <inertia> <ixx>0.2</ixx> <iyy>0.2</iyy> <izz>0.1</izz> </inertia> </inertial> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <box> <size>0.3 0.2 0.5</size> </box> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <box> <size>0.3 0.2 0.5</size> </box> </geometry> <material> <ambient>0.2 0.2 0.8 1</ambient> <diffuse>0.2 0.2 0.8 1</diffuse> </material> </visual> </link> <!-- Left Leg --> <link name="left_leg"> <pose>0 0.1 -0.25 0 0 0</pose> <inertial> <mass>3.0</mass> <inertia> <ixx>0.05</ixx> <iyy>0.05</iyy> <izz>0.01</izz> </inertia> </inertial> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <cylinder> <radius>0.05</radius> <length>0.4</length> </cylinder> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <cylinder> <radius>0.05</radius> <length>0.4</length> </cylinder> </geometry> </visual> </link> <!-- Hip Joint --> <joint name="left_hip" type="revolute"> <parent>torso</parent> <child>left_leg</child> <pose>0 0 0.2 0 0 0</pose> <axis> <xyz>0 1 0</xyz> <limit> <lower>-1.57</lower> <upper>1.57</upper> <effort>100</effort> <velocity>2.0</velocity> </limit> <dynamics> <damping>0.7</damping> </dynamics> </axis> </joint> </model> </sdf> This is a complete working model. Torso. One leg. One joint. You can extend it.
Don't edit SDF files directly. Edit URDF. Then reconvert. This keeps your workflow clean.
Check URDF first: check_urdf your_robot.urdf Fix errors before converting.
Don't convert a 100-link robot at once. Start with one link. Then two. Then three. Find problems early.
Use git. Track both URDF and SDF. This helps debugging.

You've learned URDF to SDF conversion. You understand the differences. You can convert automatically. You can fix common problems. Key points: URDF is for ROS integration SDF is for simulation Convert using gz sdf command Test thoroughly in Gazebo Fix physics issues carefully

You've learned the pieces. Now put them together. Build a complete simulation. A humanoid robot. A realistic apartment. This project combines everything. Environment modeling. Sensor integration. ROS 2 communication. By the end, you have a working digital twin.

Your project includes: A realistic apartment with multiple rooms Furniture and obstacles A humanoid robot with sensors Real-time sensor data streaming ROS 2 visualization This is a real robotics project. You could expand it for research or development.

Type: Scenario Context: You want to test a home service robot. Buying a robot costs $15,000. Breaking things costs more. Explanation: Build a digital twin first. Test in simulation. Find bugs. Fix problems. No risk. No cost. When it works, deploy to real hardware. Companies like Boston Dynamics do this. They test millions of scenarios. First in simulation. Then on real robots. This saves time. It saves money. It prevents accidents. Takeaway: Digital twins let you fail fast and cheap. Perfect your system before touching real hardware.

Start with a basic apartment layout. worlds/apartment.sdf <!-- Library: Gazebo Harmonic (osrf/gazebo latest) Last updated: 2025-12-05 Tested on: Gazebo Harmonic, Ubuntu 22.04 --> <?xml version="1.0"?> <sdf version="1.9"> <world name="apartment"> <!-- Physics settings --> <physics name="physics" type="ode"> <max_step_size>0.001</max_step_size> <real_time_factor>1.0</real_time_factor> </physics> <!-- Lighting --> <light name="sun" type="directional"> <pose>0 0 10 0 0 0</pose> <diffuse>0.8 0.8 0.8 1</diffuse> <specular>0.2 0.2 0.2 1</specular> <direction>-0.5 0.1 -0.9</direction> </light> <!-- Ground plane --> <model name="ground_plane"> <static>true</static> <link name="link"> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <plane> <normal>0 0 1</normal> </plane> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <plane> <normal>0 0 1</normal> <size>100 100</size> </plane> </geometry> <material> <ambient>0.8 0.8 0.8 1</ambient> <diffuse>0.8 0.8 0.8 1</diffuse> </material> </visual> </link> </model> <!-- Living room wall --> <model name="wall_north"> <static>true</static> <pose>0 5 1.5 0 0 0</pose> <link name="link"> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <box> <size>10 0.2 3</size> </box> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <box> <size>10 0.2 3</size> </box> </geometry> <material> <ambient>0.9 0.9 0.9 1</ambient> <diffuse>0.9 0.9 0.9 1</diffuse> </material> </visual> </link> </model> <!-- Kitchen wall --> <model name="wall_south"> <static>true</static> <pose>0 -5 1.5 0 0 0</pose> <link name="link"> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <box> <size>10 0.2 3</size> </box> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <box> <size>10 0.2 3</size> </box> </geometry> <material> <ambient>0.9 0.9 0.9 1</ambient> <diffuse>0.9 0.9 0.9 1</diffuse> </material> </visual> </link> </model> </world> </sdf> This creates a basic room. Two walls. A floor. Lighting.

Add a simple table: <!-- Add this inside <world> tag --> <model name="table"> <static>true</static> <pose>2 0 0.5 0 0 0</pose> <link name="link"> <collision name="collision"> <geometry> <box> <size>1.2 0.8 0.05</size> </box> </geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry> <box> <size>1.2 0.8 0.05</size> </box> </geometry> <material> <ambient>0.6 0.4 0.2 1</ambient> <diffuse>0.6 0.4 0.2 1</diffuse> </material> </visual> </link> </model> Add more furniture. Chairs. Shelves. A bed. Make it realistic.

Include your humanoid robot model: <!-- Add robot to world --> <include> <uri>model://my_humanoid</uri> <pose>0 0 1.0 0 0 0</pose> <name>robot</name> </include> The robot spawns in the center. One meter above ground.
Your robot needs sensors. Add them to the robot SDF.

models/my_humanoid/model.sdf <sensor name="camera" type="camera"> <pose>0.1 0 1.6 0 0 0</pose> <camera> <horizontal_fov>1.047</horizontal_fov> <image> <width>640</width> <height>480</height> </image> <clip> <near>0.1</near> <far>100</far> </clip> </camera> <update_rate>30</update_rate> <topic>/camera/image_raw</topic> </sensor> This creates a camera. It publishes to ROS 2. 30 frames per second.

<sensor name="depth_camera" type="depth_camera"> <pose>0.1 0 1.6 0 0 0</pose> <camera> <horizontal_fov>1.047</horizontal_fov> <image> <width>640</width> <height>480</height> <format>R_FLOAT32</format> </image> <clip> <near>0.1</near> <far>10</far> </clip> </camera> <update_rate>10</update_rate> <topic>/camera/depth/image_raw</topic> </sensor> This provides depth information. Essential for navigation.

<sensor name="imu" type="imu"> <pose>0 0 0.5 0 0 0</pose> <imu> <angular_velocity> <x> <noise type="gaussian"> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.01</stddev> </noise> </x> <y> <noise type="gaussian"> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.01</stddev> </noise> </y> <z> <noise type="gaussian"> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.01</stddev> </noise> </z> </angular_velocity> <linear_acceleration> <x> <noise type="gaussian"> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.1</stddev> </noise> </x> <y> <noise type="gaussian"> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.1</stddev> </noise> </y> <z> <noise type="gaussian"> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.1</stddev> </noise> </z> </linear_acceleration> </imu> <update_rate>100</update_rate> <topic>/imu</topic> </sensor> The IMU tracks orientation. It includes realistic noise.

Create a launch file. This starts everything: launch/apartment_sim.launch.py # Library: ros2 launch v3.3.7 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 from launch import LaunchDescription from launch.actions import ExecuteProcess, IncludeLaunchDescription from launch_ros.actions import Node def generate_launch_description(): return LaunchDescription([ # Start Gazebo with apartment world ExecuteProcess( cmd=['gz', 'sim', '-r', 'apartment.sdf'], output='screen' ), # Start robot state publisher Node( package='robot_state_publisher', executable='robot_state_publisher', name='robot_state_publisher', parameters=[{'robot_description': 'path/to/your/robot.urdf'}], output='screen' ), # Start RViz with config Node( package='rviz2', executable='rviz2', name='rviz2', arguments=['-d', 'config/rviz_config.rviz'], output='screen' ), ]) This launches Gazebo. It starts RViz. It publishes robot state.
ros2 launch apartment_project apartment_sim.launch.py Wait for Gazebo to load. This takes 10-30 seconds.
Verify sensors publish data: ros2 topic list You should see: /camera/image_raw /camera/depth/image_raw /imu /joint_states

Check camera images: ros2 run rqt_image_view rqt_image_view Select /camera/image_raw. You should see the robot's view. Check IMU data: ros2 topic echo /imu You should see orientation and acceleration updates.

Type: Scenario Context: Your camera shows black. No image appears. Explanation: First, check the topic. Run ros2 topic echo /camera/image_raw. If no data appears, the sensor isn't publishing. Check your SDF file. Is the camera plugin loaded? Does the topic name match? If data appears in echo but not in rqt_image_view, check the image format. RGB8 is standard. Still broken? Check Gazebo console for errors. Most problems are typos or missing plugins. Takeaway: Debugging sensors requires systematic checks. Topics, plugins, formats, and error logs.
Check simulation speed: gz topic -e -t /stats Look for real_time_factor. Should be close to 1.0. If below 0.5, your simulation is too slow.
Measure camera frame rate: ros2 topic hz /camera/image_raw Should report around 30 Hz. If lower, something is wrong.
Move the robot. Use keyboard teleop: ros2 run teleop_twist_keyboard teleop_twist_keyboard The robot should move smoothly. No jitter. No crashes.
Problem: Real-time factor below 0.5. Solutions: Reduce physics step size Simplify models (fewer polygons) Disable shadows in Gazebo Use simpler sensor configurations
Problem: Robot spawns and immediately falls. Solution: Check collision geometries. Ensure ground plane has collision element. Verify robot spawn height is correct.
Problem: Topics exist but no data. Solutions: Check plugin is loaded Verify topic names match Ensure sensors have update_rate set Check Gazebo console for errors

depth_processor.py # Library: rclpy v3.3.7, cv_bridge v3.2.1 # Last updated: 2025-12-05 # Tested on: ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from sensor_msgs.msg import Image from cv_bridge import CvBridge import cv2 class DepthProcessor(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__('depth_processor') self.subscription = self.create_subscription( Image, '/depth_camera/depth/image_raw', self.depth_callback, 10 ) self.bridge = CvBridge() def depth_callback(self, msg): depth_image = self.bridge.imgmsg_to_cv2(msg, desired_encoding='32FC1') # Process depth data here cv2.imshow('Depth', depth_image / 10.0) # Normalize for display cv2.waitKey(1) def main(): rclpy.init() node = DepthProcessor() rclpy.spin(node) node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown()

Welcome to Module 4, the culmination of our journey! Here, we bring together everything you've learned to create conversational humanoids that understand natural language commands and execute complex tasks.

VLA models represent the cutting edge of embodied AI – systems that can perceive their environment (Vision), understand human language (Language), and execute physical tasks (Action). These models bridge the gap between human communication and robot execution.
